# nylon

:::note[Hard fork]
This site documents a **hard fork** of [encodeous/nylon](https://github.com/encodeous/nylon) with fork-only additions: [AmneziaWG 2.0 traffic obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation), [runtime dynamic prefixes](/reference/dynamic-prefixes), the [`nylon-lb` LoadBalancer controller](/guides/nylon-lb), and the [`nylon-genesis` obfuscation-parameter generator](/guides/genesis). The upstream project and its original documentation remain at [github.com/encodeous/nylon](https://github.com/encodeous/nylon) and [nylon.jq.ax](https://nylon.jq.ax).
:::

Nylon is a self-healing WireGuard mesh that routes around failures. If a link goes down, nylon reroutes traffic through the next-best path in seconds. No manual intervention, no central coordination servers.

[See how nylon compares to Tailscale, Nebula, and DIY setups →](/why-nylon)

## Here's another example

Here is a network of 5 nodes, where the numbers on the edges represent the routing metric (nylon uses latency).

:::note
Nylon does not require a fully connected network. Nodes forward packets on behalf of their neighbours, so routing works as long as any path exists between two nodes.
:::

```mermaid
graph LR
    vps --- |2| charlie
    vps --- |2| alice
    eve --- |1| bob
    vps --- |5| eve
    alice --- |1| bob
```

```yaml
routers:
  - id: vps
    pubkey: dJcUE1qnXCQ5x8pMhFb/MZab7YrBaaHcrgfbmQI0MW4=
    addresses: [10.0.0.1]
    endpoints:
      - "vps.encodeous.ca"
  - id: alice
    pubkey: xmfAovAKN4AY5ocK5s+/VsG9I27KrQ13Vzb0HOsLKAs=
    addresses: [10.0.0.2]
  - id: bob
    pubkey: 4GfHHSyVpXc+wkbjyIIONERa6Xf5EafB0nVGZLf2r2o=
    addresses: [10.0.0.3]
    endpoints:
      - "192.168.1.19:57175"
  - id: charlie
    pubkey: WcCkKijU0brYnRzxk867HTDyYFf/cqiKTTOLSxtWoFc=
    addresses: [10.0.0.4]
  - id: eve
    pubkey: 2mXTTD+FYdtJm/v1vSHz8qimvCucjW9vY+nLYacXJFE=
    addresses: [10.0.0.5]

graph:
  - trio = alice, charlie, eve
  - vps, trio
  - bob, eve
  - bob, alice
```

From `alice`, nylon selects the path of least metric to each destination (highlighted):

```mermaid
graph LR
    vps --- |2| charlie
    vps --- |2| alice
    eve --- |1| bob
    vps --- |5| eve
    alice --- |1| bob
    linkStyle 0 stroke:#4caf50,stroke-width:2px
    linkStyle 1 stroke:#4caf50,stroke-width:2px
    linkStyle 2 stroke:#4caf50,stroke-width:2px
    linkStyle 4 stroke:#4caf50,stroke-width:2px
```

If the `alice - bob` link goes down, the network automatically reconfigures around the failure:

```mermaid
graph LR
    vps --- |2| charlie
    vps --- |2| alice
    eve --- |1| bob
    vps --- |5| eve
    alice --- |1| bob
    linkStyle 0 stroke:#4caf50,stroke-width:2px
    linkStyle 1 stroke:#4caf50,stroke-width:2px
    linkStyle 2 stroke:#4caf50,stroke-width:2px
    linkStyle 3 stroke:#4caf50,stroke-width:2px
    linkStyle 4 stroke:#e53935,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:5
```

url: /why-nylon

# Why Nylon?

Nylon is a self-healing WireGuard mesh that routes around failures. If a link goes down, nylon reroutes traffic through the next-best path in seconds. No manual intervention, no central coordination servers.

Under the hood, nylon implements the machinery of the [Babel routing protocol (RFC 8966)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8966) over a custom in-band protobuf control plane — not wire-interoperable with Babel daemons — on top of a [modified wireguard-go](https://github.com/Arsolitt/nylon/tree/main/polyamide), using measured latency as the routing metric for learned mesh links (some advertised prefixes carry static or health-check metrics), with damped switching (~10% deadband, 5 s hold).

### Main Features

- **Multi-hop Routing**: Traffic flows through the lowest-latency path across your mesh. Unlike Tailscale, Nebula, or ZeroTier, nodes don't need to be directly reachable from each other. Nylon forwards through intermediate hops automatically.
- **No Coordination Server**: No SaaS dependency, no single control-plane. Nodes exchange routes directly over the same WireGuard tunnel that carries your data.
- **Single Daemon Binary, Single Port**: One statically-linked daemon binary, one UDP port (set `port` in node.yaml — there is no code default; `57175` is the convention and the fallback for endpoints without a port), one YAML config per node (node.yaml), plus the shared central.yaml, which the daemon can bootstrap from node.yaml's `dist` block on first start. That's all a node runs. Optional companion tools: `nylon-genesis` as a raw binary in the same release (generates the mesh-wide `obf` profile and per-node I1-I5 obfuscation parameters) and `nylon-lb` as a container image only (anycast LoadBalancer VIPs).
- **WireGuard Client Compatibility**: On meshes running the vanilla compatibility profile, stock WireGuard clients (iOS, Android, Windows) join with zero extra software, and mobile clients roam between gateways seamlessly. Obfuscated (AmneziaWG) profiles change the handshake format, so stock clients cannot connect to obfuscated nodes — see [Traffic Obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation).
- **Native WireGuard Speeds**: Data-plane runs entirely in `wireguard-go` (polyamide), so forwarded traffic stays on the WireGuard data path with no extra proxy hop.

## Comparison

| Feature               | **nylon**                                      | **Tailscale**                            | **Nebula**              | **DIY WG+Babel**                      |
| :-------------------- | :--------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------- | :---------------------- | :------------------------------------ |
| **Topology**          | **Partial mesh: nodes forward for each other** | Full mesh (every pair needs a tunnel)    | Full mesh               | Partial mesh (manual setup)           |
| **Routing**           | **Latency-aware, automatic multi-hop**         | No routing (relay only, no optimization) | No routing              | Yes (depends on daemon)               |
| **Self-healing**      | **Yes — mesh links heal in seconds**           | Relies on coordination server            | No automatic failover   | Yes (depends on daemon)               |
| **Coordination**      | **None required (fully in-band)**              | Centralized (SaaS/Headscale)             | Lighthouse servers      | Manual (out-of-band protocol)         |
| **WireGuard Clients** | **Stock iOS/Android/Windows clients work**     | Tailscale client only                    | Nebula client only      | Manual configuration                  |
| **NAT Traversal**     | Port forward or public relay node              | **STUN/ICE/DERP (best-in-class)**        | Public lighthouse nodes | Manual                                |
| **Configuration**     | Central YAML file                              | Web Dashboard / SSO                      | Certificates & CA       | Multiple configs + network namespaces |
| **License**           | Apache 2.0                                     | Proprietary SaaS / BSD-3 client          | MIT                     | Various                               |

Healing times depend on what failed. Measured by the fork maintainer in proof-of-concept testing: a broken mesh link heals in about **3 seconds**. Routes announced through dynamic prefix announcements (for example, Kubernetes pod CIDRs) converge in **20–25 seconds** — the route lags the mesh heal while Babel resolves the sequence-number request cycle. And when the original link comes back, restoring the direct path can take a couple of minutes (**102 s** observed) while Babel ages the stale route.

:::caution[Encryption Model]
Nylon uses WireGuard's encryption **hop-by-hop**, not end-to-end. Each link between adjacent nodes is encrypted, but intermediate nodes decrypt and re-encrypt forwarded traffic. This is the same model as DIY WireGuard+Babel setups. If you need end-to-end encryption between every pair of nodes, Tailscale or Nebula may be a better fit.
:::

## When to use nylon

- **Distributed edge nodes**: Build low-latency anycast networks for geographically distributed services that adapt to changing conditions.
- **Home lab networking**: Connect home devices, servers, and cloud resources into a single resilient network.
- **Sovereign networks**: Fully independent mesh that works in isolated or air-gapped environments. No "phone-home" requirement.
- **Optimized routing**: Automatically use the lowest-latency path without manual configuration changes.

## Nylon vs. DIY WireGuard+Babel

If you've ever tried to build a dynamic network using WireGuard + Babel (or BGP), you know how powerful it can be, but also how painful it is to maintain.

[The typical setup](https://forum.mikrotik.com/t/best-approach-to-mesh-y-vpn-with-ospf/175811) involves running separate WireGuard interfaces for every peering arrangement, along with a routing daemon to manage dynamic routing. This gives you a powerful, self-healing network, but it's cumbersome to set up and maintain.

**Nylon is that powerful DIY stack refined into a single, opinionated binary.** It automates the tedious parts, giving you the resilience of a professional routing setup with the ease of a modern VPN.

# Getting Started

This guide will walk you through setting up a basic nylon network with two nodes.

```mermaid
graph LR
    node1(node-1<br/>10.0.0.1) <--> node2(node-2<br/>10.0.0.2)
```

## Prerequisites

- Two machines with UDP port `57175` open (can configure with a different port).
- The `nylon` binary downloaded on both machines from the [releases page](https://github.com/Arsolitt/nylon/releases).

:::note
The Linux and macOS versions are well tested. The fork maintainers report that the Windows TUN interface has stability issues, so for Windows we recommend using [WireGuard for Windows](https://www.wireguard.com/install/) and connecting to a Linux/macOS machine as a [passive client](/guides/wg-clients).
:::

1. **Generate Keypairs**

   On each node, generate a WireGuard keypair:

   ```bash
   nylon key
   ```

   This will output two keys (example):

   ```text
   kPoLiC4+Nh9AoQGiBmJTh+8BUqCMsa6Zdr4M0Xz5bX0=
   9Z1HGi7eip6GdQezqy3Vc7Er76ZgTfryda9wvHUgWzk=
   ```

   The first key (stdout) is your private key, and the second key (stderr) is your public key. Keep the private key safe, and note down the public key for the next step.

   :::tip
   If you already have a WireGuard keypair, you can use that interchangeably with nylon.
   :::

2. **Create Node Configuration**

   On each node, create a `node.yaml` file. Replace `<YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY>` with the private key generated in step 1.

   ```yaml
   id: node-1 # Give each node a unique ID (e.g., node-1, node-2)
   key: <YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY>
   port: 57175
   ```

3. **Create Central Configuration**

   The `central.yaml` file defines the topology of your network. Create one file and share it across all nodes.

   ```yaml
   routers:
     - id: node-1
       pubkey: <NODE_1_PUBLIC_KEY>
       endpoints:
         - "node1.example.com:57175" # could be a domain name
         - "192.168.1.2:57175" # could be a local ip
       addresses:
         - 10.0.0.1 # this is the internal nylon IP
     - id: node-2
       pubkey: <NODE_2_PUBLIC_KEY>
       endpoints:
         - "node2.example.com:57175"
       addresses:
         - 10.0.0.2

   # Define the connections between nodes
   graph:
     - node-1, node-2 # This means node-1 and node-2 will try to connect to each other
   ```

4. **Validate your configuration**

   Before launching, you can check that your config files are correct:

   ```bash
   nylon verify central.yaml --node node.yaml
   ```

5. **Launch nylon**

   Run nylon on both machines:

   ```bash
   sudo nylon run -c central.yaml -n node.yaml
   ```

   After a few seconds, the nodes will discover each other and establish a secure tunnel. You should be able to ping `10.0.0.2` from `node-1`.

## Next Steps

- Learn how to connect [Passive Nodes](/guides/wg-clients) to support edge platforms like iOS.
- Discover how to use [Config Distribution](/guides/config-distribution) to manage your network configuration with ease.
- Setup nylon without a static public IP using [Dynamic DNS & Port Forwarding](/guides/port-forward).
- Monitor your nodes with [Prometheus metrics and health checks](/guides/observability).
---

---
# WireGuard Clients

One of nylon's key features is compatibility with standard WireGuard clients (iOS, Android, Windows, etc.). These are called **Passive Nodes/Clients**.

:::caution
Stock WireGuard clients interoperate with a nylon mesh **only** when it uses a vanilla-compatible obfuscation profile (the default). Without an `obf` section in `central.yaml`, nylon pins the handshake headers to `h1=1-1` through `h4=4-4` — the vanilla WireGuard message types — so the mesh speaks byte-compatible vanilla WireGuard. The same byte-compatibility can be pinned explicitly with `nylon-genesis --compat`. If your mesh enables a profile that deviates from these vanilla-pinned values, stock WireGuard clients cannot complete handshakes with nylon peers. See [Obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation) for how profiles work.
:::

## How it Works

Passive nodes do not participate in the routing protocol. Instead, they connect to a **Gateway Node** (a regular nylon node) which advertises their presence to the rest of the network.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Nylon Mesh"
        N1[Node A]
        N2[Node B]
        N3[Node C]
        N1 <--> N2
        N2 <--> N3
        N3 <--> N1
    end
    subgraph "Passive Clients"
        P1[WireGuard iOS Client]
        P2[WireGuard Android Client]
        P3[WireGuard Windows Client]
    end
    P1 <--> N1
    P2 <--> N2
    P3 <--> N2
```

1. **Configure the Passive Node**

   Use any WireGuard app to generate a keypair. Note the public key.

2. **Update Central Configuration**

   Add the passive node to your `central.yaml`. Passive nodes should **not** have endpoints.

   ```yaml
   routers:
     - id: node-1
       pubkey: <GATEWAY_NODE_PUBLIC_KEY>
       addresses: [10.0.0.1]
       endpoints:
         - "node1.example.com:57175"
     # ... other routers ...

   clients:
     - id: my-phone
       pubkey: <PHONE_PUBLIC_KEY>
       addresses:
         - 10.0.0.5

   graph:
     - node-1, my-phone # Connect the passive node to a gateway node
   ```

3. **Connect to a Gateway**

   In your WireGuard app, set the `Endpoint` to the address of a router that is graph-adjacent to this client (an edge such as `node-1, my-phone` in `central.yaml`). A router with no graph edge to the client never creates its WireGuard peer and drops its handshakes.

   ```ini
   [Interface]
   PrivateKey = <PHONE_PRIVATE_KEY>
   Address = 10.0.0.5/32

   [Peer]
   PublicKey = <GATEWAY_NODE_PUBLIC_KEY>
   Endpoint = gateway.example.com:57175
   AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.0/24 # or whatever you want to route through nylon
   ```

## Limitations

- A single WireGuard peer entry in a client app has one active `Endpoint` at a time — this is standard client-side WireGuard behaviour, not a mesh constraint. The mesh itself accepts a passive client adjacent to multiple gateways; to reach several of them, configure multiple profiles sharing the same private key (see [Dynamic Routing](#dynamic-routing)).
- They cannot forward traffic for other nodes.
- They rely on the gateway node for connectivity to the rest of the network.

## Dynamic Routing

Even though passive nodes do not participate in routing, they can still benefit from nylon's dynamic routing capabilities. By configuring multiple VPN profiles using the same private key, a client can switch between gateways automatically.

:::tip
Depending on the WireGuard app, there may be features like Scene-based routing in [Shadowrocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadowrocket) that can automatically switch the gateway node/VPN profile based on network conditions.

This can help your passive node maintain optimal connectivity, even when you travel.
:::

### No Keepalive Needed

:::note

You do not need to enable Persistent Keepalive, or any heartbeat mechanism for this simple use case.

:::

When a gateway is the **sole advertiser** of a passive client's prefix, nylon retains the route for that client indefinitely, ensuring it remains reachable even if it goes idle for an extended period. The indefinite hold starts from the last live advertisement: a configured client that has not sent a packet since the gateway (re)started is not advertised until it does — any authenticated packet, including a keepalive, bootstraps it. The hold is skipped while another gateway's advertisement or route for the prefix is visible (a route with a finite metric from a different source); graph adjacency alone does not suppress it — the competing advertisement, refreshed by the gateway that now holds the client, is what ends the hold. Refreshes continue while the client keeps talking (silence under `ClientDeadThreshold`, 6 s); the last refresh sets the 3-second advertisement TTL, and the 1-second garbage collection removes the lapsed advertisement — so the prefix is withdrawn roughly 8-10 seconds after the client's last packet. With multiple gateways, enable Persistent Keepalive to keep the route alive during idle periods, with an interval faster than `ClientDeadThreshold` (6 s default) — 5 s as used by the passive-roaming e2e test, since the commonly recommended 25-second Persistent Keepalive is too slow and the route lapses; the conservative bound is under `ClientKeepaliveInterval` (3 s). With a sole-advertising gateway, you should only enable Keepalive if:

1. You need other nodes to be able to initiate connections to the client after long periods of silence.
2. You really wish to drain the battery of the client device for some reason...

For mobile devices, leaving Keepalive disabled is recommended to maximize battery life.

> For a deep dive into how nylon handles roaming and keeps idle clients reachable, see the [Passive Nodes Reference](/reference/passive-nodes).

# Config Distribution Setup

Nylon's distribution system allows you to manage network topology from a central source using signed and encrypted "bundles".

```mermaid
graph TD
    Admin[Admin] -- "nylon seal & upload" --> S3[("S3 Bucket / Web Server (central.nybundle)")]

    subgraph "Nylon Mesh"
        NodeA[Node A]
        NodeB[Node B]
    end

    S3 -- "Fetch & Update" --> NodeA
    S3 -- "Fetch & Update" --> NodeB
```

:::caution
Despite being called a "public" key, the distribution key also acts as the shared secret for decrypting your network config. To keep your internal network structure private, only share this key with the nodes in your network.
:::

1. **Generate a Distribution Keypair**

   First, generate a keypair specifically for distribution (separate from node keys).

   ```bash
   nylon key > dist.key 2> dist.pub
   ```

2. **Seal your Configuration**

   Sign and encrypt your `central.yaml` into a `.nybundle` file.

   ```bash
   nylon seal -c central.yaml -k dist.key -o central.nybundle
   ```

3. **Publish the Bundle**

   Host `central.nybundle` on any HTTP/HTTPS server (e.g., GitHub Pages, S3, or Nginx).

4. **Configure Nodes**

   **Initial Bootstrap (`node.yaml`)**

   Nodes fetch their first central config using the `dist` block:

   ```yaml
   dist:
     url: "https://your-server.com/central.nybundle"
     key: "<contents-of-dist.pub>"
   ```

   The `dist` block in `node.yaml` is bootstrap-only: it is consulted only when `central.yaml` does not exist yet. Afterwards it is ignored, and updates flow solely from the `dist` block in `central.yaml`; a corrupt `central.yaml` is not replaced from `node.yaml`.

   **Automatic Updates (`central.yaml`)**

   Once bootstrapped, nodes poll the repositories defined in `central.yaml`:

   ```yaml
   dist:
     key: "<contents-of-dist.pub>"
     repos:
       - "https://your-server.com/central.nybundle"
   ```

   Nylon polls for updates every 10 seconds, but applies a bundle only when its timestamp is strictly newer than the active config. `nylon seal` rewrites that timestamp to the sealing host's wall clock, so each seal is newer by construction; re-uploading an older bundle is ignored, and clock skew on the sealing host can block rollout.

## Key rotation

When `dist` is configured, `dist.key` must be set to a nonzero public key. To rotate it, put the new public key in `central.yaml` and sign that bundle with the old private key. That transition seal deliberately logs the warning `bundled public key differs from the signing key, check if this is intended!`, because the bundle is sealed with the old key (so old-key nodes can open it) while already carrying the new `dist.key`. After nodes apply the bundle, sign subsequent updates with the new private key; seals with the new key no longer warn.
---

# Port Forwarding

While nylon can often route traffic through intermediate nodes to overcome NAT issues, **port forwarding** is necessary when your nodes cannot establish any direct, or indirect path due to restrictive NATs.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Home Network A"
    A[Node A]
    end
    subgraph "Home Network B"
    B[Node B]
    end
    A <--> NAT1((NAT))
    NAT2((NAT)) <--> B
    NAT1 -.-|Inaccessible| NAT2
```

## Do I Need to Port Forward?

Connectivity in nylon depends on whether at least one node in a peering pair is publicly reachable.

| Your Setup | Port Forwarding? | Reason |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Node ↔ Public Server** | Not Required | The node behind NAT can connect directly to the public server. |
| **Nodes across multiple NATs** | **Required** | If both nodes are behind NATs (e.g., two different home networks) and there are no other publicly accessible ports, the graph will be disconnected. |

By forwarding a port on at least one node, you ensure that nodes across different networks can always find a path to each other, preventing "isolated islands" in your mesh.

:::tip[Similar to BitTorrent]
If you've ever used BitTorrent, this is the same as being **"connectable."** Just as two "unconnectable" torrent peers cannot share files with each other, two nylon nodes across different NATs cannot establish a tunnel unless at least one of them has an open port.
:::

## Configuration Steps

1. **Configure Your Router/Firewall**

   Log into your router or firewall and create a port forwarding rule:
   - **External Port**: `57175`
   - **Internal Port**: `57175`
   - **Protocol**: `UDP`
   - **Internal IP**: The local IP address of the machine running nylon.

2. **Handle Dynamic IPs (DDNS)**

   If your home or office has a dynamic public IP address, you should use a **Dynamic DNS (DDNS)** service. This ensures that even when your IP changes, other nodes can still find you.

   Popular tools like [ddclient](https://github.com/ddclient/ddclient) can automatically update your DNS records (e.g., Cloudflare, Namecheap, DuckDNS) whenever your public IP changes. Your router may also have built-in DDNS support.

3. **Update Central Configuration**

   Once the port is forwarded and your DNS is set up, tell the rest of the network how to reach this node by adding an `endpoint` to your `central.yaml`.

   ```yaml
   routers:
     - id: home-server
       pubkey: <HOME_SERVER_PUBLIC_KEY>
       endpoints:
         - "home.example.com" # Your DDNS hostname
       addresses:
         - 10.0.0.1
   ```

   Alternatively, publish the node as a DNS SRV record. When nylon resolves an endpoint hostname, it first looks up a `_nylon._udp.<hostname>` SRV record; if one exists, the record's target and port are used, taking precedence over the hostname's A/AAAA records. The forwarded port then lives in DNS instead of `central.yaml`, so it can be changed by updating the record alone:

   ```text
   _nylon._udp.home.example.com. 0 IN SRV 10 10 57175 home.example.com.
   ```

   The SRV target must itself have an A/AAAA record, and the record is looked up again on every endpoint re-resolution, so DDNS-style updates to it are picked up automatically.

   :::tip
   Nylon re-resolves DNS endpoints automatically: a background sweep runs every 15 seconds and a resolved address is cached for 1 minute, so a DDNS record change is picked up within about 15 seconds once the cached value is older than a minute. While a refresh is in flight (DNS queries time out after 5 seconds) and after a dropped link, nodes keep using the last known good address until a refresh succeeds.
   :::

4. **Apply Configuration**

   Ensure your changes are pushed to your configuration repository or updated on your nodes. Nylon will automatically detect the new endpoints and attempt to establish connectivity.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I need to forward ports on every node?
**No.** Nylon only needs *at least one* node with a public endpoint (either via port forwarding or a public static IP) to act as a point of entry for the mesh. However, the more nodes that have open ports, the more connected and resilient your network becomes.

### What if I use a different port?
If you use a custom port, you should configure it in your `node.yaml` (for local port), specify it in the `endpoints` section of your node in `central.yaml` (for forwarded port), and update your router's port forwarding rule accordingly.

**node.yaml**

```yaml
id: my-node
port: 12345 # This should match the internal port you forwarded
```

**central.yaml**

```yaml
routers:
  - id: my-node
    ...
    endpoints:
      - "home.example.com:12345" # This should match the external port you forwarded
```

:::note
An endpoint written without a port — a bare hostname or a bare IP address — silently falls back to the default port `57175`. If the external port you forwarded differs from the default, always write the endpoint with an explicit port, as shown in the `central.yaml` tab above.
:::

# Observability

Nylon can expose an HTTP server for Prometheus metrics, health checks, and service discovery.

## Enable the server

Set `observability_addr` in each node's `node.yaml`:

```yaml
observability_addr: "0.0.0.0:9090"
```

Restart nylon after changing the node configuration. You can then check the local node:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:9090/healthz
curl http://127.0.0.1:9090/readyz
curl http://127.0.0.1:9090/metrics
```

:::caution
The observability server does not provide authentication or TLS. Bind it to a trusted interface, or protect it with a firewall or authenticated reverse proxy. Avoid exposing it directly to the internet.
:::

## Endpoints

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/healthz` | Returns `200 OK` while the daemon is running and `503 Service Unavailable` while it is shutting down. |
| `/readyz` | Returns `200 OK` when nylon's internal event loop responds, or `503 Service Unavailable` if it cannot respond within one second. It does not check whether every peer is reachable. |
| `/metrics` | Returns metrics in the Prometheus text exposition format. Returns `503 Service Unavailable` if nylon cannot collect a status snapshot within one second. |
| `/discovery` | Returns Prometheus HTTP service-discovery targets for the addresses in `central.yaml`. |

## Configure Prometheus

For a single node, add a static scrape target in `prometheus.yml`:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: nylon
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "10.0.0.1:9090"
```

For a mesh, Prometheus can discover the node addresses from any nylon observability server. Add the following to `prometheus.yml`:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: nylon
    http_sd_configs:
      - url: "http://10.0.0.1:9090/discovery"
        refresh_interval: 30s
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: [nylon_node_type]
        regex: passive
        action: drop
```

The discovery response uses every node address from `central.yaml`. Each target has a `nylon_node` label containing the node ID and a `nylon_node_type` label set to either `router` or `passive`. The example drops passive targets because they do not run the nylon daemon.

Configure the same observability port on every router, and make sure Prometheus can reach their nylon addresses on that port.

## Metrics

All metric names start with `nylon_`.

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nylon_build_info` | Gauge | `version`, `commit` | Build metadata for the running daemon; always `1`. |
| `nylon_up` | Gauge | — | `1` when nylon can produce a metrics snapshot. |
| `nylon_config_timestamp_seconds` | Gauge | — | Unix timestamp of the active central configuration. |
| `nylon_neighbours` | Gauge | — | Number of configured neighbours. |
| `nylon_active_endpoints` | Gauge | — | Number of active peer endpoints. |
| `nylon_selected_routes` | Gauge | — | Number of selected Babel routes. |
| `nylon_advertised_prefixes` | Gauge | — | Number of locally advertised prefixes. |
| `nylon_wireguard_transmit_bytes_total` | Counter | — | WireGuard bytes transmitted by this node. |
| `nylon_wireguard_receive_bytes_total` | Counter | — | WireGuard bytes received by this node. |
| `nylon_wireguard_peer_transmit_bytes_total` | Counter | `peer` | WireGuard bytes transmitted to a peer. |
| `nylon_wireguard_peer_receive_bytes_total` | Counter | `peer` | WireGuard bytes received from a peer. |
| `nylon_wireguard_peer_latest_handshake_seconds` | Gauge | `peer` | Unix time of the peer's latest WireGuard handshake, or `0` before the first handshake. |
| `nylon_endpoint_active` | Gauge | `peer`, `endpoint` | `1` when the endpoint is active, otherwise `0`. |
| `nylon_endpoint_metric` | Gauge | `peer`, `endpoint` | Current Babel endpoint metric. |
| `nylon_endpoint_rtt_seconds` | Gauge | `peer`, `endpoint` | Filtered endpoint round-trip time in seconds. |
| `nylon_route_metric` | Gauge | `prefix`, `router`, `next_hop` | Metric of a selected Babel route. |

For example, alert when a node cannot be scraped or when a peer has not completed a handshake in the last five minutes:

```text
up{job="nylon"} == 0
```

```text
time() - nylon_wireguard_peer_latest_handshake_seconds > 300
```

The handshake metric is `0` before the first successful handshake, so this expression also selects peers that have never connected. When using it in an alerting rule, add `for: 5m` to avoid firing while nylon starts and establishes its initial peer connections.

### Performance gauges

Nylon exports its hot-loop performance counters on `/metrics` as `nylon_perf_*` metrics, plus three monotonic `nylon_tun_*_drops_total` counters. The windowed values are computed over a rolling 10-second window and exposed as gauges, because windowed values are not monotonic; the one exception is `nylon_perf_dispatch_latency_us`, which uses a 1-minute window. Metrics with a `quantile` label (`0.5`, `0.9`, `0.99`) report the p50, p90, and p99 over the window.

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nylon_perf_dispatch_latency_us` | Gauge | `quantile` | Main-loop dispatch latency in microseconds; p50/p90/p99 over a rolling 1-minute window. |
| `nylon_perf_send_batch_size` | Gauge | `quantile` | Packets per send batch. |
| `nylon_perf_recv_batch_size` | Gauge | `quantile` | Packets per receive batch. |
| `nylon_perf_tun_read_batch_size` | Gauge | `quantile` | Packets per TUN read call. |
| `nylon_perf_tun_write_batch_size` | Gauge | `quantile` | Packets per TUN write call. |
| `nylon_perf_sends_per_second` | Gauge | — | WireGuard sends per second. |
| `nylon_perf_recvs_per_second` | Gauge | — | WireGuard receives per second. |
| `nylon_perf_sent_packets_per_second` | Gauge | — | Packets sent per second. |
| `nylon_perf_recv_packets_per_second` | Gauge | — | Packets received per second. |
| `nylon_perf_sent_bytes_per_second` | Gauge | — | Bytes sent per second. |
| `nylon_perf_recv_bytes_per_second` | Gauge | — | Bytes received per second. |
| `nylon_tun_staged_drops_total` | Counter | — | Packets evicted from a per-peer staged queue because they were too old. |
| `nylon_tun_write_queue_drops_total` | Counter | — | Bounce packets dropped because the target TUN writer queue was full. |
| `nylon_tun_kernel_tx_dropped_total` | Counter | — | Kernel `tx_dropped` counter of the TUN interface, sampled from `/sys/class/net/<iface>/statistics/tx_dropped`. |

Despite their `_per_second` names, these gauges are not normalized rates: each value is the count accumulated over the rolling 10-second window. Divide by 10 for an approximate per-second value.

Unlike the gauges above, the three `nylon_tun_*_drops_total` counters are monotonic totals rather than windowed values. `nylon_tun_kernel_tx_dropped_total` is a ten-second sysfs sample of `/sys/class/net/<iface>/statistics/tx_dropped`: the kernel counter is monotonic only for the lifetime of the interface, so it resets to zero when the interface is recreated, and the exported value is the last successful sample. If these counters grow, the TUN drain is the bottleneck, not the network: `staged` counts packets evicted from a bounded per-peer userspace queue (the reader outran a peer), `write_queue` counts bounce batches dropped before reaching a TUN writer, and `kernel` counts packets the kernel could not hand to the daemon at all.

These metrics are always available on `/metrics`; `--dbg-perf` is only required for the standalone debug server on port `6060`, which serves the performance web UI and `pprof` endpoints. The debug server's `/debug/metrics` page additionally lists the TUN totals as `tun:stagedDrops`, `tun:writeQueueDrops`, and `tun:kernelTxDropped`.

## Logging

Nylon writes structured logs to stderr. Every record carries a `component` attribute (`nylon`, `nylon-lb`, or `nylon-genesis`) and, for the daemon, a `node` attribute containing the node ID. Subsystem records add a `module` attribute, for example `router`, `polyamide`, `ipc`, `dynamic-prefixes`, `prefix-health`, or `observability`.

Readiness transitions are logged once per state change, not per probe: when a ready node starts failing its readiness check, nylon logs `readiness failed` at warn level, and logs `readiness recovered` at info level when the check passes again.

To keep logs on disk, set `log_path` in `node.yaml` (or pass `--log <file>` (`-l`) to `nylon run`). The file sink is written in JSON format, one record per line, so it can be ingested directly by log processors. See [Troubleshooting](/guides/troubleshooting) for log level control and day-to-day debugging.
---
url: /guides/troubleshooting
---
# Troubleshooting

## Control logging

The log level is resolved in this order (first match wins):

1. `--log-level` flag (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`) on `nylon run` and `nylon-lb`.
2. `NYLON_LOG_LEVEL` environment variable, with the same values.
3. `-v`/`--verbose`, a shorthand for `debug`.
4. The default, `info`.

An unknown value in the flag or the environment variable is rejected at startup.

Other output controls:

- `--json` writes JSON records to stderr instead of the default colored text output.
- `log_path` in `node.yaml` (or `nylon run --log <file>` (`-l`)) additionally writes logs to a file. The file sink is always JSON, one record per line.

To set the level for a systemd service:

**nylon.service**

```ini
[Service]
Environment=NYLON_LOG_LEVEL=debug
```

## Read the logs

Records are structured and attributable: `component` identifies the binary (`nylon`, `nylon-lb`, `nylon-genesis`), `node` carries the node ID, and `module` names the subsystem (`router`, `polyamide`, `ipc`, `dynamic-prefixes`, `prefix-health`, `observability`, `allocator`, `speaker`).

The router logs its decisions with an `event` attribute, at these levels:

| Event | Level | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `route_inserted`, `route_updated`, `route_retracted`, `route_expired` | Debug | Babel route lifecycle. |
| `seqno_requested` | Debug | A sequence number was requested from a neighbour. |
| `major_route_change` | Info | A significant change in the selected route set. |
| `inconsistent_state` | Warn | The router detected inconsistent state. |
| `no_endpoint_to_neighbour` | Warn | A neighbour has no usable endpoint. |

At the default `info` level you see topology changes and problems, but not individual route updates — raise the level to `debug` while investigating.

## Collect a snapshot for bug reports

`nylon techinfo` produces a single JSON document on stdout combining the node's full status with a connectivity probe of every neighbour:

```bash
nylon techinfo -i nylon0
```

A one-line human summary goes to stderr. Attach the JSON output and a short log excerpt (with `--log-level debug` if possible) to your bug report. The command exits non-zero if the status request fails.

## Inspect a running node

Every command in this table except `nylon verify` talks to the daemon over its IPC socket, so it works only while the daemon is up. When the daemon is not running — or `-i` names the wrong interface — the command exits 1. On Linux with the default interface name, it prints:

```text
Error: connect to nylon: dial unix /var/run/wireguard/nylon.sock: connect: no such file or directory
```

The socket is named after the daemon's real interface (`<iface>.sock` under `/var/run/wireguard`): on macOS that is the kernel-assigned `utunN.sock` — pass that name to `-i` — and on Windows the endpoint is a named pipe (`\\.\pipe\ProtectedPrefix\Administrators\WireGuard\<name>`) instead.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `nylon status` | Neighbours and selected routes (`--routes` for route tables, `--full` for routing internals). |
| `nylon probe <peer>` | Probe connectivity to one peer (`--timeout`, default `2s`; values above `10s` are silently capped). |
| `nylon trace` | Live stream of the daemon's packet-routing decisions. Requires the daemon to have been started with `--dbg-trace-tc`; otherwise it fails with `Error: tracing not enabled; restart with --dbg-trace-tc`. |
| `nylon reload` | Re-read the central config from disk without a restart; prints `Result: NOOP\|APPLIED\|RESTART_REQUIRED` (plus `Message:` when set), and on `REJECTED` exits 1 with an `Error:` line. The `--file` flag is accepted but ignored. |
| `nylon verify <central-config>` | Validate configs without starting the daemon (`--node <node-config>` also checks a node config); prints `Config is valid` or `Error: <reason>`. |

`status`, `probe`, and `trace` accept `-i/--interface` (default `nylon`); `status` and `probe` also accept `--json` for machine-readable output; `reload` accepts `-i/--interface` and `--json` as well (with `--json` it prints the raw response as JSON). `trace` accepts no other flags.

## Debug flags

Flags for `nylon run`:

- `--dbg-perf` starts a debug server on port `6060` with the performance web UI and `pprof` endpoints.
- `--dbg-trace` writes a Go runtime trace to `trace.out`; inspect it later with `go tool trace`.
- `--dbg-trace-tc` traces the daemon's packet-routing decisions; `nylon trace` streams them live. `nylon status` reports `trace enabled` based on this flag only — setting `--dbg-trace` does not affect it.
- `--dbg-wg` enables WireGuard (polyamide) logs. They are emitted at info level, so they appear at the default log level.
- `--dbg-probe` (`-p`) writes probe debug lines (`probe from`, `probe back`) at Debug level; needs `--log-level debug` to be visible.
- `--dbg-repo` logs stale repo bundles (`found old update bundle at <repo>, skipping`) at Debug level; also needs `--log-level debug`.

## Metrics quick pointers

- Alert when a peer goes silent: `time() - nylon_wireguard_peer_latest_handshake_seconds > 300`. See [Observability](/guides/observability) for the full expression and its caveats.
- Check hot-loop health with the `nylon_perf_*` gauges: dispatch latency and batch size quantiles (a 1-minute window for dispatch latency, 10 s for the rest), plus send/receive values that are counts accumulated over the 10-second window, not per-second rates.

## Debugging nylon-lb

The load balancer uses the same log controls (`--log-level`, `NYLON_LOG_LEVEL`, `-v`, `--json`), and Kubernetes client-go/klog messages are routed into the same log.

- `nylon_lb_leader` is `1` on the instance currently holding the leader lease.
- `/healthz` is a liveness probe: it returns 200 once the process is serving. `/readyz` returns 503 until the informer caches have synced — point your readiness probe at `/readyz`.
- `/metrics` exposes leader, allocation, and announce counters and gauges for scraping.
---
url: /guides/obfuscation
---
# Traffic Obfuscation

Vanilla WireGuard is easy to recognize on the wire. Every handshake packet starts with a fixed 4-byte message type (1 through 4) and has fixed sizes, so deep packet inspection (DPI) can identify and block WireGuard connections even though their content is encrypted. Nylon's obfuscation layer — wire-compatible with the AmneziaWG 2.0 format — lets you reshape that traffic so the mesh no longer looks like WireGuard.

Obfuscation changes the shape of handshake packets:

- **Junk packets** — meaningless packets sent before a handshake; receivers discard them without validating them. Each junk datagram's length is drawn uniformly from the half-open range `[jmin, jmax)` — `jmax` itself is never emitted, and equal bounds give fixed-length junk.
- **Custom type words** — each handshake message carries a type word drawn from a range you choose instead of the fixed 1–4.
- **Custom padding** — each handshake message type is padded to a size you choose.
- **Protocol templates** — initiation packets can be laid out to imitate another protocol such as QUIC, so a packet capture reads like ordinary application traffic.

Obfuscation does **not** change anything else: the cryptography, the key exchange, and routing are exactly the same as vanilla WireGuard. Only the byte layout of packets on the wire differs.

## Configuration Surface

Obfuscation is configured at two levels in `central.yaml` (see [Configuration Reference](/reference/config) for the full field documentation):

| Level | Fields | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Central `obf` profile | `jc`, `jmin`, `jmax`, `s1`–`s4`, `h1`–`h4` | One shared profile for the whole mesh |
| Per-node `obf` (`routers[].obf`, `clients[].obf`) | `protocol`, `i1`–`i5` | Sender-local, may differ per node |

A minimal central profile with a per-node QUIC-style template:

```yaml
obf:
  jc: 5
  jmin: 250
  jmax: 800
  s1: 32
  s2: 28
  s3: 20
  s4: 16
  h1:
    min: 100
    max: 5000000
  h2:
    min: 10000000
    max: 200000000
  h3:
    min: 400000000
    max: 800000000
  h4:
    min: 1000000000
    max: 2100000000
routers:
- id: node1
  obf:
    protocol: quic
    i1: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0040><b 0x00><b 0x01><t><r 40>
    i2: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><d><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0020><b 0x01><t><r 20>
    i3: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0010><b 0x01><t><r 10>
    i4: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0005><b 0x01><t><r 5>
```

### The Central Profile Must Match Mesh-Wide

The `s1`–`s4` and `h1`–`h4` values are a wire contract between every pair of nodes:

- A **sender** picks each outgoing message's type word from its own `h` ranges and pads the message by its own `s` values.
- A **receiver** classifies incoming packets using **its own** `s`/`h` values.

If two nodes carry different `s`/`h` values, the receiver fails to classify the sender's packets and drops them silently. The junk-packet knobs `jc`, `jmin`, `jmax` are not part of that wire contract — junk datagrams are sender-local camouflage that receivers discard unclassified — but they cannot diverge either: they exist only in the single central `obf` profile, which is distributed identically to every node. [nylon-genesis](/guides/genesis) enforces this by construction.

### I-Patterns Are Sender-Local

The `i1`–`i5` patterns (and the informational `protocol` label) describe only what **this node sends**. You never configure another node's I values anywhere, and receivers do not validate your patterns against their own. This is why two nodes can use different I-patterns — for example, different templates per site — while staying fully interoperable, as long as their central `s`/`h` profiles match.

## The Default Profile Is Vanilla-Compatible

If you omit the `obf` section entirely, nylon does **not** disable the obfuscation machinery. It pins the header ranges to the exact vanilla WireGuard message types — `h1=1-1` through `h4=4-4` — with zero padding, no junk packets, and no I-patterns. The mesh speaks byte-compatible vanilla WireGuard.

:::caution
This is deliberately **not** the AmneziaWG "all zeros" default, which would produce a type word of 0 and break interoperability with vanilla WireGuard. The converse also holds: any profile that deviates from these vanilla-pinned values breaks stock-client handshakes. To pin the vanilla-compatible values explicitly — for example across a version-skew window during a rollout — [nylon-genesis](/guides/genesis) `--compat` emits a profile with exactly these ranges (and zero padding, no junk packets, no I-patterns). The vanilla-compatible profile is the **only** mode in which a stock WireGuard client (iOS, Android, Windows, …) can complete a handshake with a nylon peer. See [WireGuard Clients](/guides/wg-clients).
:::

In practice:

- Run the default (no `obf` section) if you need stock-client support anywhere in the mesh.
- Enable an obfuscated profile only when every participant — every nylon node and every client — speaks the obfuscated format.

## Initiation Packet Patterns

Each `i1`–`i5` value is a pattern built from tags. Each tag describes one stage of the packet, and nylon renders the packet by concatenating every tag's output in order:

| Tag | Produces |
| --- | --- |
| `<b 0x…>` | Fixed bytes written verbatim, e.g. `<b 0xc0ff>` |
| `<r n>` | `n` random bytes |
| `<rd n>` | `n` random digits |
| `<rc n>` | `n` random letters |
| `<t>` | The current Unix timestamp as a 4-byte big-endian value |
| `<d>` | The packet's own data, passed through unchanged |
| `<ds>` | The packet's own data, base64-encoded |
| `<dz n>` | An `n`-byte field encoding the data size |

In nylon, chains are rendered only for I-packet camouflage, and there the data source is empty: `<d>` and `<ds>` therefore contribute zero bytes, and `<dz n>` contributes `n` zero bytes. The QUIC-template `i2` in the example above renders 36 bytes on the wire — 8 bytes shorter than the upstream template's intent, because upstream assumes `<d>` re-uses the 8-byte connection ID that `i1` carries.

Each pattern renders one pre-handshake camouflage datagram: `i1`–`i5` are sent in order ahead of every handshake initiation, followed by the `jc` junk datagrams and only then the real initiation message — none of them replaces or shapes an actual handshake message. Reading the `i1` example above: it opens with fixed bytes that imitate the target protocol's header, injects random bytes, carries a timestamp, and ends with trailing random bytes — so each camouflage datagram has the length and layout of the chosen template rather than of WireGuard.

:::note
No I-pattern content is verified when a packet is received: the live receive path classifies packets purely by size and by the `h` ranges of the mesh-uniform central profile, matching upstream AmneziaWG 2.0 behavior. The patterns shape what a node sends; the cryptography — not the pattern — provides authenticity.
:::

### Validation Limits

Nylon rejects invalid profiles at apply time rather than producing a broken mesh:

- Header ranges (`h1`–`h4`) must not overlap each other; an overlapping set fails at apply with the error `headers must not overlap`.
- Genesis-generated header ranges must stay clear of the vanilla WireGuard type ids 1–4. This clearance is enforced at generation time by [nylon-genesis](/guides/genesis); a hand-written `central.yaml` overlapping 1–4 is not rejected at apply.
- AmneziaWG 3.x-only parameters (`header_protection_key`, `content_padding_addition`, `random_trailers`, `disable_cookies`, `rekey_after_time`, `rekey_timeout`, `reject_after_time`, `keepalive_timeout`, and `max_handshake_attempts`) are rejected only at the device UAPI boundary, where the parser fails them with `UAPI knob %q is AWG 3.x-only and unsupported by this AWG 2.0 build`. They are not `central.yaml` fields — the config decoder silently ignores unknown YAML keys, so a hand-written 3.x parameter under `obf:` is ignored, not rejected. No non-2.0 wire format can be activated.

## Generating Profiles with nylon-genesis

Hand-writing a mesh-consistent profile is error-prone: one wrong `h` range on a single node blackholes that node's traffic. [nylon-genesis](/guides/genesis) is the recommended way to produce obfuscation config:

- It generates the central `obf` profile and per-node I-patterns together, so the mesh-uniform values match by construction.
- It offers named protocol templates (for example `quic`) that fill in realistic `i1`–`i4` patterns like the ones shown above.
- Empty I-specs are never emitted, and `i5` stays empty for the named templates.

If you are bootstrapping a new mesh, generate the config first and tune the obfuscation knobs in the generated file.

## Operational Notes

- **Profile switches are a maintenance event.** A changed profile applies live on config sync, but handshakes already in flight can fail for up to one rekey window while nodes converge on the new layout. Schedule profile changes accordingly.
- **A brief packet loss at startup is benign.** Right after a profile change, packets sealed with the pre-profile layout are dropped and then retransmitted under the new one; connectivity recovers on its own.
- **Correctness is pinned by tests.** The obfuscation layer is validated against golden vectors from upstream amneziawg-go (46 vectors over 3 profiles, pinned to a fixed upstream revision), and an interop harness runs nylon against an in-process reference device built from the upstream amneziawg-go implementation (`github.com/amnezia-vpn/amneziawg-go/v3`) over real UDP:

```bash
go test -tags awg_ref_interop ./interop/awgref/
```

See [Development](/guides/development) for the harness tags and how to run the interop suite.
---
url: /guides/genesis
---
# Config Genesis

`nylon-genesis` is the internal companion tool that generates obfuscation parameters for a nylon mesh. It asks the [amnezigo](/guides/development) parameter oracle for a validated shared profile, generates per-node handshake camouflage, and writes the result as a paste-ready YAML fragment for your `central.yaml`: a top-level `obf:` block plus `routers:` entries that carry only `id` and `obf`.

The tool generates obfuscation parameters only. WireGuard keys are a separate concern handled by `nylon key` — see [Getting started](/guides/getting-started).

## What nylon-genesis generates

Every run emits one fragment with two parts:

- A mesh-wide shared profile under `obf:` — the junk (`jc`, `jmin`, `jmax`), padding sizes (`s1`–`s4`), and message-type header ranges (`h1`–`h4`) that every node in the mesh must share.
- One `routers:` entry per node you list, each carrying only that node's `id` and its sender-local `obf` block with `i1`–`i5` CPS strings.

The fragment unmarshals cleanly into the central config structure, but it does not merge itself — you paste it into `central.yaml` by hand (see [Generate a profile](#generate-a-profile)). The shared profile is mesh-uniform by construction: one oracle call fixes S/H/J for the whole mesh, and every node receives every peer's `i1`–`i5` spec through the central config while sending only with its own.

The following output is the real committed fixture from this repository, generated with the command shown in Step 5. Each additional id you pass to `--peers` appends another entry with the same shape:

```yaml
obf:
  jc: 5
  jmin: 250
  jmax: 800
  s1: 32
  s2: 28
  s3: 20
  s4: 16
  h1:
    min: 100
    max: 5000000
  h2:
    min: 10000000
    max: 200000000
  h3:
    min: 400000000
    max: 800000000
  h4:
    min: 1000000000
    max: 2100000000
routers:
- id: node1
  obf:
    protocol: quic
    i1: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0040><b 0x00><b 0x01><t><r 40>
    i2: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><d><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0020><b 0x01><t><r 20>
    i3: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0010><b 0x01><t><r 10>
    i4: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0005><b 0x01><t><r 5>
```

For the meaning of each field, see [Obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation).

## Build the tool first

`nylon-genesis` is built from the same repository as the daemon; it links the GPL-3.0 [`amnezigo`](https://github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo) oracle, which `go.mod` pins as an ordinary module dependency — the Go toolchain downloads it during the build, nothing extra to check out.

```bash
make build
```

`make build` produces `bin/nylon-genesis` alongside `bin/nylon` and `bin/nylon-lb`. Running `go run ./cmd/nylon-genesis` from the repository works identically.

## Generate a profile

1. **Choose the shared profile source**

   Decide where the mesh-wide S/H/J parameters come from:

   - **Preset** (default): a named amnezigo preset, `standard-1420` by default. The preset supplies the junk and padding profile and the default MTU.
   - **Random**: pass `--random` to have the oracle generate a random profile instead. The preset still provides the default MTU and contributes `s1` and `jc`; `s2`–`s4`, `h1`–`h4`, and the `jmin`/`jmax` junk range are drawn fresh. A draw can collide a peer's `i1`–`i5` packet length with one of the profile's padded handshake sizes, which the AWG 2.0 size invariant forbids; the generator redraws a whole random profile when that is what is random, and always redraws a peer's `i`-set, until it validates (64 attempts, then an error) — with the default `--protocol random` that combination failed about half the time before the redraw.

2. **Choose a protocol template**

   `--protocol` selects the camouflage template for the per-node handshake packets: `quic`, `dns`, `dtls`, `stun`, `sip`, `rtp`, or `random` (the default). Named protocols use that protocol's template shape and fill `i1`–`i4`; `i5` is intentionally left empty. `random` does not pick a template — it generates randomized simple CPS patterns across all of `i1`–`i5`, including `i5`.

3. **Choose an MTU clamp (optional)**

   `--mtu` bounds only the generated per-node I-packet sizes to your underlay MTU (the oracle caps each I-packet at `mtu - 49 - 149 - s1`). Junk sizes are not clamped — they come from the preset, or from a fresh 64–1024 byte draw under `--random` — so a small `--mtu` can still emit junk datagrams large enough to fragment. Leave it at the default `0` to use the preset's default MTU — `standard-1420` targets a 1420-byte underlay, and the fixture output above was generated with `--mtu 1420`.

4. **List your nodes**

   `--peers` takes a comma-separated list of node ids. Use the same ids your routers carry in `central.yaml`, because you will merge each generated block into the matching router entry.

5. **Run the tool**

   ```bash
   bin/nylon-genesis --preset standard-1420 --protocol quic --mtu 1420 --peers node1,node2
   ```

   The fragment goes to stdout. Pass `--out obf-fragment.yaml` to write it to a file instead (mode `0644`), and `-v`/`--verbose` for debug logging on stderr:

   ```bash
   bin/nylon-genesis --protocol quic --peers node1,node2 --out obf-fragment.yaml -v
   ```

6. **Merge the fragment into central.yaml**

   Paste the `obf:` block at the top level of `central.yaml`, then merge each `routers:` entry into your existing `routers:` list:

   ```yaml
   # Top level: paste the generated obf block verbatim.
   obf:
     jc: 5
     # ... rest of the generated obf block ...

   routers:
     - id: node1
       # Keep every existing key of this router and add obf alongside them.
       obf:
         protocol: quic
         i1: <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0040><b 0x00><b 0x01><t><r 40>
         # ... i2, i3, i4 from the generated fragment ...
   ```

   The full field semantics — what S/H/J do on receive, why S/H must match mesh-wide, and how sender-local `i1`–`i5` are used — are covered in [Obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation), and the complete field reference lives in [Configuration reference](/reference/config).

   :::caution
   The fragment does not merge itself. Each `routers:` entry contains only `id` and `obf`, so never paste the fragment's `routers:` list over your existing one — merge each `obf` block into the matching node's entry and keep that node's other keys intact.
   :::

7. **Distribute and reload**

   Ship the updated `central.yaml` to your mesh the same way you distribute any config change — via [config distribution](/guides/config-distribution) or a direct reload. Nodes pick up the new profile on their next config sync.

   :::caution
   Treat an obfuscation profile rollout as a maintenance action. The new parameters apply live when each node syncs, but in-flight handshakes can fail for one rekey window during the transition.
   :::

## Flag reference

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--preset` | `standard-1420` | amnezigo preset name for the shared profile. |
| `--random` | `false` | Generate a random shared profile via amnezigo's `GenerateConfig` instead of the preset; the draw is redrawn until it satisfies the size-classification invariant (64 attempts, then an error). |
| `--protocol` | `random` | Per-peer I1–I5 template: `quic`, `dns`, `dtls`, `stun`, `sip`, `rtp`, or `random`. |
| `--mtu` | `0` | Underlay MTU clamp for I-packet sizes only; `0` uses the preset default. |
| `--peers` | empty | Comma-separated node ids to generate per-node I1–I5 for. |
| `--compat` | `false` | Emit the fixed vanilla-compat profile; the output does not depend on `--preset` or `--protocol`, but they are still validated. |
| `--out` | stdout | Write to `FILE` instead of stdout (file mode `0644`). |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | `false` | Log debug detail to stderr. |

Print the stamped build version with the `--version` flag: `nylon-genesis --version` outputs `nylon-genesis version dev` (`dev` for local builds without version ldflags). There is no `version` subcommand — an unknown positional word is not an error, so `nylon-genesis version` silently generates a full obfuscation profile on stdout.

## Vanilla compatibility (--compat)

Pass `--compat` to generate the vanilla-compat profile instead of an obfuscated one. It pins `h1`–`h4` to the exact vanilla WireGuard message types and leaves everything else at zero — no junk, no padding, and no per-node `obf` blocks. This is the profile that keeps stock WireGuard clients working against your mesh during a version-skew window:

```yaml
obf:
  h1:
    min: 1
    max: 1
  h2:
    min: 2
    max: 2
  h3:
    min: 3
    max: 3
  h4:
    min: 4
    max: 4
routers:
- id: node1
- id: node2
```

Two things to know about this mode:

- The compat output does not depend on `--preset` or `--protocol`, but they are still validated: an unknown value fails before any output is produced.
- It deliberately skips the header-range viability checks that normal generation runs, because pinning headers to 1–4 is exactly what those checks reject: obfuscated ranges must stay clear of the vanilla message types.

If your whole mesh speaks vanilla WireGuard anyway, you can also omit the `obf` key from `central.yaml` altogether — a mesh with no profile pins the same 1–4 header types. See [Obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation) for the profile semantics, and [WireGuard clients](/guides/wg-clients) for attaching stock clients to a mesh.

## Validation and failure behavior

Before writing anything, the tool validates its own output:

1. Structural checks on the profile: `jmin` must not exceed `jmax`, and every `h1`–`h4` range must have `min` no greater than `max`.
2. Per-header range viability via the amnezigo validator.
3. The packet-size classification invariant for the S-padded handshake sizes and the junk range.
4. A re-check of the freshly generated per-peer `i1`–`i5` lengths.

An unknown `--protocol` or `--preset` name fails before any output is produced, so a failed run never leaves a half-written `--out` file behind.

## Provenance and licensing

`nylon-genesis` links the GPL-3.0 [`amnezigo`](https://github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo) parameter oracle, so a `nylon-genesis` binary is a GPL-3.0 combined work: if you distribute it, you must pass on the GPL-3.0 terms and the corresponding source — this repository plus amnezigo, both of which are public. The repository's own source files keep their source licenses (Apache-2.0 at the root, MIT for `polyamide/`), and the nylon daemon links only MIT-licensed device code and Apache-2.0 nylon code — it carries no copyleft obligations.

For build requirements, see [Building and testing](/guides/development).
---
url: /guides/nylon-lb
---
# Kubernetes LoadBalancer

`nylon-lb` gives Services of `type=LoadBalancer` real, reachable addresses inside a nylon mesh. It watches those Services, allocates a free IPv4 address from a pool you configure, writes the address into the Service's `status.loadBalancer.ingress`, and announces the address as a `/32` into the mesh by writing a file to the [dynamic prefixes directory](/reference/dynamic-prefixes). Cilium running in kube-proxy-replacement mode consumes `status.loadBalancer.ingress` and steers traffic to the Service.

`nylon-lb` owns no datapath. Forwarding happens in the node's existing network stack; the controller only allocates addresses, and the speaker only makes the mesh aware of them.

## Architecture

One binary contains two components that you can enable and disable independently:

- **Allocator** — runs once per cluster. It watches Services only, picks the lowest free address from the Service's selected pool for each LoadBalancer Service, and writes it to `status.loadBalancer.ingress` with single-object compare-and-swap updates. The allocator runs under leader election with a Lease named `nylon-lb-allocator`; the CAS status writes keep a partitioned ex-leader from corrupting anything.
- **Speaker** — runs on every node. It watches Services and EndpointSlices, which is why `/readyz` waits for both informer caches to sync; for each Service the node should announce, it binds the allocated address to the loopback interface (Linux netlink) and writes an announce file into the prefixes directory. Speakers are never leader-elected: every node announcing the same `/32` is the design, and Babel treats the copies as anycast.

## Command-line flags

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--pool` | required | Named IPv4 pool to allocate LoadBalancer addresses from, as `name=cidr` (e.g. `shared=192.0.2.0/24`). Repeat the flag for each pool. |
| `--exclude` | none | Excludes addresses from the pool. Repeat the flag as needed. |
| `--lb-class` | none | `loadBalancerClass` to claim. Empty claims all `type=LoadBalancer` Services; set it to scope nylon-lb to its own class and coexist with other LB controllers. |
| `--prefixes-dir` | `/etc/nylon/prefixes.d` | Directory the speaker writes announce files into. |
| `--bind-interface` | `lo` | Interface to bind announced addresses to. Set it empty (`--bind-interface=`) to disable binding. |
| `--kubeconfig` | none | Path to a kubeconfig file. |
| `--node-name` | hostname | Name of this node. Must match the Kubernetes node name for `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` to work. |
| `--leader-elect` | `true` | Leader-elect the allocator. |
| `--leader-namespace` | ServiceAccount namespace, else `kube-system` | Namespace for the leader-election Lease. |
| `--resync` | `30s` | Informer resync period. |
| `--health-addr` | `:9633` | Listen address for `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and `/metrics`. Set it empty to disable the server. |
| `--speaker` | `true` | Enable the per-node announcer. |
| `--allocator` | `true` | Enable the leader-elected IP allocator. |
| `--log-level` | `$NYLON_LOG_LEVEL`, else `info` | Log level. |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | off | Verbose logging. |
| `--json` | off | Emit logs as JSON. |

Logs are structured and carry the component name `nylon-lb`, `node=<name>`, and a module (`allocator` or `speaker`). Messages from klog (client-go) are bridged into the same log pipeline.

## Allocation rules

- nylon-lb claims **every** Service of `type=LoadBalancer` in the cluster **unless `--lb-class` scopes it**: with the flag set, only Services whose `spec.loadBalancerClass` matches exactly are claimed — unclassed Services are left pending for another controller.
- Every Service selects its pool with the `nylon.io/lb-pool` annotation. Selection is fail-closed: a Service with no annotation (`MissingPoolAnnotation` event) or naming an unknown pool (`UnknownPool` event) gets no address and stays `<pending>`; an ingress address previously allocated for it is released.
- A `spec.loadBalancerIP` set on a Service is honored when the address is free and inside the selected pool.
- Allocation picks the lowest free address in the selected pool.
- The taken set is global across all pools, so overlapping pools never hand out the same address twice.
- An `--exclude` address applies to every pool that contains it.
- The pool prefix must be at least a `/30`: the network and broadcast addresses are never allocated, so smaller pools have nothing to hand out.
- Allocation is **derived, not stored**. nylon-lb recomputes the mapping from live Services on every resync and keeps no state anywhere, so deleting a Service frees its IP unconditionally. The only residual window is announce-file withdrawal lag on a down speaker node: the stale announce file persists until that node's next resync, when the stale-announce garbage collection withdraws it. There is no collision risk, because announce files are garbage-collected together with the Service.
- Kubernetes events are emitted on the Service with a pinned, machine-readable reason vocabulary: `Allocated`, `Released`, `AllocationFailed` (the selected pool is exhausted — the Service stays pending and allocation retries with backoff until an address frees up), `BadLoadBalancerIP` (a `spec.loadBalancerIP` request rejected as outside the selected pool or already taken — a pool address is allocated instead), `MissingPoolAnnotation`, and `UnknownPool`. The reasons are stable so external tooling can rely on them.
- IPv4 only.

## Announcement semantics

### Announce files

For every Service it should announce, the speaker writes one file named `lb-<namespace>-<service>.json` into `--prefixes-dir`:

```json
{"version":1,"prefixes":[{"type":"static","prefix":"192.0.2.10/32","metric":0}]}
```

The file is compact JSON plus a trailing newline. The `lb-` prefix is the garbage-collection boundary: nylon-lb removes exactly the files it owns and never touches anything else in the directory, such as `00-vip.json`.

Writes are atomic (write to a temp file, then rename). The temp file deliberately does not end in `.json`, because the nylon daemon globs `*.json` in that directory. Files whose content did not change are not rewritten, so the watcher sees no churn.

### externalTrafficPolicy

The Service's `spec.externalTrafficPolicy` decides which nodes announce:

- `Cluster` (default) — every node announces every Service `/32`. Babel treats the identical prefixes as anycast, so when a node dies, traffic simply flows to the remaining announcers. Failover is free.
- `Local` — only nodes that hold at least one ready local endpoint announce the Service. An endpoint with no `Ready` condition counts as ready.

### Single announcer

Anycast is the default because it fails over for free, but a flow that must not move — a database endpoint in the middle of `pg_basebackup`, say — is better served by one stable announcer. The `nylon.io/announce: single` annotation pins exactly one:

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    nylon.io/announce: single
spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
```

With `Local` and `single`, exactly one of the nodes holding a ready local endpoint announces the Service. Each speaker computes the winner from the sorted eligible node list itself — FNV-1a 64 of `"ns/name"` modulo the list length — so no coordination is needed and no node can disagree about who wins for a given set of endpoints. Moving the ready endpoint to another node moves the announcement with it, but because the winner is an index into the eligible list, any change to that set (a node joining or leaving it) can reshuffle which node wins.

The elected node withdraws its announcement when its own direct API view is more than 30 seconds stale — an unreachable API server means it can no longer be sure it is still the only owner. For a stateful path a bounded black-hole is preferable to two announcers, so the withdrawal is deliberately fail-closed; it is lifted as soon as a probe succeeds again.

`single` requires `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`: the eligible set comes from EndpointSlices, and with the `Cluster` policy there is no node-local set to elect from. A Service with `single` and `Cluster` is announced anycast, with a warning. Any unrecognised value is treated the same way.

:::caution[Always pass --node-name]
`deploy/daemonset.yaml` exports a `NODE_NAME` environment variable but does **not** pass `--node-name=$(NODE_NAME)` in the container args. Without the flag, nylon-lb falls back to the hostname, which does not match the Kubernetes node name inside a DaemonSet pod — so with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` no node ever matches its local endpoints, and nothing gets announced. Add `--node-name=$(NODE_NAME)` to `args` in the DaemonSet before you rely on `Local` mode.
:::

### Reconcile order

The speaker's ordering is load-bearing. It binds the address to the loopback interface **before** writing the announce file, so the address already exists on the node by the time the `/32` propagates (about 250 ms after the file lands, per the prefix watcher debounce). When withdrawing a Service, it removes the announce file **before** unbinding the address.

The unbind itself waits out a **60-second drain window**. The mesh needs a moment to converge on the withdrawal, and unbinding the instant the file disappears would black-hole flows it still routes to this node. A Service that becomes announced again during the window keeps its address: the pending drain is cancelled.

## Requirements and caveats

- **Configure every pool in every receiver.** Each pool must sit inside `dynamic_prefix_ranges` in every receiver's `central.yaml`. Receivers fail closed: announcements for prefixes outside their configured ranges are dropped. See the [configuration reference](/reference/config) and the [dynamic prefixes reference](/reference/dynamic-prefixes).
- **Scope it with `--lb-class` to coexist.** With `--lb-class` set, nylon-lb owns only Services carrying that `loadBalancerClass`, and other class-scoped LoadBalancer controllers (servicelb, MetalLB, kube-vip) may run beside it; every other controller in the cluster must also be class-scoped, and unclassed Services stay `<pending>`. With the flag empty, nylon-lb claims every LoadBalancer Service and must be the only LoadBalancer controller in the cluster.
- **IPv4 only.** No IPv6 pools.
- **Run the identical pool set on every replica.** Every replica (all DaemonSet pods or bare-binary instances) must run the same `--pool` flags with the same `--exclude` addresses; each Service picks its pool with the `nylon.io/lb-pool` annotation.

## Deployment

### Use the released image

Releases publish the controller image as `ghcr.io/arsolitt/nylon/nylon-lb`: GoReleaser tags each release with `:<version>`, and stable releases also move `:latest`. The shipped DaemonSet manifest consumes this image, so the install below needs no image build of your own; use the make targets in the next section only if you want to ship a custom image.

### Build and push the image

```bash
make image-nylon-lb
make push-nylon-lb
```

`make image-nylon-lb` builds a local, native-platform image with a plain `docker build`; only `make push-nylon-lb` builds multi-arch, via `docker buildx build --push`. The runtime image is built from `scratch` and exposes port 9633. A debug variant based on `ubuntu:24.04` is available with `make image-nylon-lb-debug`.

### Install with the shipped manifests

```bash
kubectl apply -f cmd/nylon-lb/deploy/rbac.yaml
kubectl apply -f cmd/nylon-lb/deploy/daemonset.yaml
```

`rbac.yaml` creates a ServiceAccount and a ClusterRole with get/list/watch on Services and EndpointSlices, update on `services/status`, get/create/update on Leases, and create/patch on Events.

`daemonset.yaml` runs one pod per node in `kube-system`, tolerates control-plane nodes, mounts the prefixes directory from a hostPath, and runs as root (`runAsUser: 0`) with `NET_ADMIN` — both are required for the netlink bind. The manifest sets `hostNetwork: true` with `dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet` (the latter keeps cluster DNS resolvable), so the speaker runs in the node's network namespace and the announced `/32`s are bound on the node's `lo` rather than the pod's — which is what makes the node answer for the addresses it announces. Cilium in kube-proxy-replacement mode steers traffic using `status.loadBalancer.ingress`. Liveness and readiness probes target port 9633.

Before you enable `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, add `--node-name=$(NODE_NAME)` to `args` in the DaemonSet as explained in the caution above.

### Allocator-only replica

An allocator-only replica needs neither root nor `NET_ADMIN`:

```bash
nylon-lb --pool=shared=192.0.2.0/24 --allocator=true --speaker=false --bind-interface=
```

### Run as a bare binary

You can run the binary directly instead of using the DaemonSet — for example under systemd, one instance per node:

```bash
nylon-lb \
  --pool=shared=192.0.2.0/24 \
  --prefixes-dir=/etc/nylon/prefixes.d \
  --node-name=node-1 \
  --kubeconfig=/etc/nylon/kubeconfig
```

Point `--prefixes-dir` at the directory your nylon daemon watches and set `--node-name` explicitly. A speaker still needs root or `CAP_NET_ADMIN` for the loopback bind. The bind is implemented with netlink and exists on Linux only: on other platforms nylon-lb refuses to start when `--bind-interface` is set (`netlink binder requires Linux`), so pass `--bind-interface=` to run a speaker without binding.

## Observability

See [Observability](/guides/observability) for wiring these signals into your monitoring stack.

### Metrics

All metrics are exposed at `/metrics` on `--health-addr` with the `nylon_lb_` prefix:

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nylon_lb_build_info` | gauge | `version`, `commit` | Build identification. |
| `nylon_lb_leader` | gauge | `node` | 1 while this replica holds the allocator Lease. |
| `nylon_lb_allocated_ips` | gauge | — | Pool addresses currently allocated to owned LoadBalancer Services (`status.loadBalancer.ingress`) — the VIPs this controller has handed out. |
| `nylon_lb_services` | gauge | — | LoadBalancer Services owned by this controller. |
| `nylon_lb_announces` | gauge | — | Desired `/32` announcements for this node, recomputed each speaker reconcile (intended, not a count of successful binds or writes). |
| `nylon_lb_allocations_total` | counter | — | Address allocations. |
| `nylon_lb_releases_total` | counter | — | Ingress clearances on type change or pool-annotation failure. |
| `nylon_lb_announce_writes_total` | counter | — | Successful announce-file sync calls, including unchanged no-op calls: it advances per desired announce per reconcile (~30 s resync) even when nothing on disk changes. |
| `nylon_lb_errors_total` | counter | `kind` | Errors by kind: `bind`, `write`, `reconcile`, `list`, `glob`. |

`nylon_lb_services` and `nylon_lb_allocated_ips` are cluster-wide: every replica derives them from the same Service informer cache and reports identical values, so aggregate them with `max`, never `sum`. Their difference is the number of managed Services still waiting for an address — a Service with a missing or unknown pool annotation, an exhausted pool, or a status write not yet observed.

Note that `nylon_lb_releases_total` does not move when a Service is deleted: once the Service is gone from the lister there is no ingress left to clear, and the stale announce file is withdrawn by the speaker's garbage collection instead.

### Health endpoints

- `/healthz` — liveness. Returns 200 as soon as the HTTP server is serving.
- `/readyz` — readiness. Returns 503 `informer caches not synced` until the Service and EndpointSlice informer caches have synced, then 200.
- `/metrics` — Prometheus text format.

## Shipped implementation vs. the design doc

:::note
`design.md` §6 sketches an earlier LoadBalancer design: a ConfigMap state store, finalizers, writes to `spec.externalIPs`, and single/anycast mode flags. None of that shipped. The controller in `cmd/nylon-lb/` derives allocation from live Services, selects the announcing nodes through `spec.externalTrafficPolicy`, and elects a single announcer with the `nylon.io/announce: single` annotation.
:::
