url: /guides/development
---
# Building & Testing

Everything in nylon's development workflow routes through one file: the `Makefile`. You build with `make build` (or the per-binary targets `make nylon`, `make nylon-genesis`, `make nylon-lb`), run tests with `make test*`, regenerate protobufs with `make proto`, and cut container images with `make image-nylon-lb`. This page walks through the prerequisites, every make target, the build tags that gate each test suite, and how releases and the demo tooling work.

## Prerequisites

- **Go 1.26.3** — the toolchain is pinned to this exact version in `mise.toml`, `go.mod`, the root `Dockerfile`, and `cmd/nylon-lb/Dockerfile.dev`, and every CI job resolves it through `actions/setup-go` with `go-version-file: go.mod`, so every environment builds with the same compiler.
- **Docker** — required for the e2e suite, which runs real containers through [testcontainers](https://go.testcontainers.org/). The unit and integration suites do not need it.

The Makefile exports `CGO_ENABLED=0` for all builds, so you get fully static binaries without touching your shell environment.

For the configs that `nylon-genesis` generates, see the [genesis guide](/guides/genesis).

## Make Targets

| Target | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `make build` | Builds `bin/nylon`, `bin/nylon-genesis`, and `bin/nylon-lb`, stamping version/commit via `-ldflags` (`git describe` / `git rev-parse`). |
| `make nylon` | Builds `bin/nylon` only, from `./cmd/nylon`. |
| `make nylon-genesis` | Builds `bin/nylon-genesis` only, from `./cmd/nylon-genesis`. |
| `make nylon-lb` | Builds `bin/nylon-lb` only, from `./cmd/nylon-lb`. |
| `make test` | Runs `gotestsum --race -tags=router_test ./...` — the tagged Babel scenarios plus all untagged unit tests (core and `polyamide/`). |
| `make test-integration` | Runs the in-process integration suite (`--race -tags=integration ./integration/...`) — needs no Docker. |
| `make test-e2e` | Runs the e2e suite (`-tags=e2e ./e2e/... -parallel $(NPROC)`) — requires Docker. |
| `make test-all` | Runs all three suites in sequence. |
| `make notice` | Regenerates `NOTICE` and `licenses/` via `go run ./hack/noticegen` — CI's licenses job fails when they are stale. |
| `make proto` | Runs `go generate ./cmd/nylon` to regenerate `protocol/*.pb.go`. |
| `make image-nylon-lb` | Builds the `nylon-lb` container image (runtime stage of `cmd/nylon-lb/Dockerfile.dev`). |
| `make image-nylon-lb-debug` | Builds the debug variant of the same `Dockerfile.dev` (debug stage: `ubuntu:24.04` plus `curl`, `iproute2`, and `tcpdump`). |
| `make push-nylon-lb` | Rebuilds the `nylon-lb` runtime image multi-platform (`$PLATFORMS`) via `buildx --push` and pushes it to `$REGISTRY` — it does not push the local image left behind by `make image-nylon-lb`. |
| `make clean` | Removes `bin/`. |

After `make build`, you have all three binaries in `bin/`. To configure and run the daemon, continue with [Getting Started](/guides/getting-started).

## Build Tags

All test-only code sits behind build tags. The `interop/awgref` package (`awg_ref_interop`) and the `sys_virtual` layer (`integration`) stay out of a default `go build ./...` — the production `sys_physical` layer is the inverse (`!integration`), so it is always part of the default build and only swaps out for `sys_virtual` when the integration suite runs.

| Tag | Gates |
| --- | --- |
| `router_test` | The core routing test suite: the 30 Babel scenario tests in `core/router_test.go` (including the `RouteSwitchHold`/deadband cases) plus their `core/router_harness.go` scaffolding — the only two files carrying this tag. The `sys_route`, `nylon_tc`, `nylon_scheduler`, `future`, `observability`, `ipc_handler`, `nylon_apply`, `system_apply`, `dynamic_prefixes`, `router_log`, and `nylon_wireguard` tests are untagged, as are all `polyamide/...` tests, and run under any `go test`. |
| `integration` | The `./integration/...` suite: an in-process `VirtualHarness` built on `ChannelTUN` with configurable latency/jitter/loss links, checked for leaks with `goleak.VerifyNone`. |
| `e2e` | The `./e2e/...` suite: full multi-node scenarios in Docker via testcontainers. |
| `awg_ref_interop` | The `interop/awgref` interoperability suite, which validates nylon's [obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation) extensions against the reference AmneziaWG implementation. Not wired into any make target or CI job — run it manually with `go test -tags awg_ref_interop ./interop/awgref/ -v -count=1`. |

### The `nylon-debug` Image

The e2e suite needs a test-node image with real networking tools. Before any e2e test runs, `TestMain` pre-builds a `nylon-debug:latest` image from the `debug` target of the root `Dockerfile`: an unpinned `ubuntu:latest` base plus `iputils-ping`, `iperf3`, `curl`, `iproute2`, `iptables`, `jq`, `fping`, `mtr-tiny`, `wireguard-tools`, `net-tools`, `tcpdump`, `dnsutils`, `netcat-openbsd`, `tmux`, `asciinema`, and `python3`. Expect the first `make test-e2e` run to take longer while this image builds.

The e2e harness also allocates its Docker networks dynamically: it picks a free `10.200`–`10.250.x.x/24` subnet at runtime so the suite never collides with networks you already have.

## Test Suites

### Unit: `make test`

Runs `./...` with the `router_test` tag enabled and the race detector on — the tagged Babel routing scenarios plus every untagged unit test in `core/` (route-table handling, traffic-control plumbing, the scheduler, observability, IPC handlers, config apply, dynamic prefixes, and more) and all of `polyamide/`. This is the fastest feedback loop and needs no Docker.

### Integration: `make test-integration`

Starts real nylon logic against an in-process virtual network, so there are no TUN devices, no root, and no Docker. The harness wires nodes together over `ChannelTUN` links with tunable latency, jitter, and loss, and every test asserts clean shutdown with `goleak`.

What the suite covers:

- Basic lifecycle and connectivity: `TestStartStop`, `TestSimplePing`, `TestSimpleRoutedPing`.
- Best-path selection under faster probes: `TestOptimalConvergence`.
- In-process routing, TUN-less relay forwarding, and TTL expiry: `TestInProcessRouting`, `TestInProcessRoutingThroughTUNLessRelay`, `TestTTL`.
- Wire-format behavior: `TestAckRetractSentOnWire`.
- Central config application: live neighbour removal, restart-required local-node removal, and key rotation that keeps the next hop (`TestApplyCentralConfig*`).
- Dynamic prefixes: writing to `prefixes.d` announces a prefix, deleting it retracts it (`TestDynamicPrefixAnnounceAndWithdraw`).
- The full IPC matrix: status, probe timeout, reload, non-neighbour rejection, trace-disabled, malformed input, and clean no-errno responses (`TestIPC*`).
- Race safety under rapid config applies (`TestRapidToggleConfig`).

### E2E: `make test-e2e`

Boots multi-node topologies as Docker containers (the `nylon-debug` image from above) and asserts on real traffic. Tests run in parallel across your CPU count.

| Scenario | What it proves |
| --- | --- |
| `TestConnectivity` | A 3-node line graph converges and pings across. |
| `TestRecoveryExample` | Blackholing the alice→bob route forces a reroute via vps; pings recover. |
| `TestEndpointResolution` | Nodes resolve endpoints from CoreDNS A and SRV records. |
| `TestDynamicResolution` | A DNS record change at runtime re-resolves the endpoint to the new IP. |
| `TestProbeReportsResolvedDNSAndLatency` | Probe JSON shows `resolved=` and latency on a REPLIED hop. |
| `TestProbeReportsResolveErrorForMissingDNS` | A missing DNS record yields a resolve-error status. |
| `TestProbeReportsTimeout` | An unreachable hop yields a timeout status. |
| `TestObfProfileConnectivity` | A genesis fixture obfuscation profile connects 2 nodes over obfuscated wire, with startup retransmit retry. |
| `TestPassiveRoaming` | A kernel WireGuard client container roams node3→node2 and pings recover. |
| `TestTUNLessRelay` | A `no_tun` relay forwards traffic; the TTL-expired hop shows up in traces. |
| `TestDistribution` | A sealed bundle served by a lightweight Python HTTP server container applies on a new timestamp. |
| `TestDistributionKeyRotation` | A bundle signed with the old key installs a new distribution key; the next bundle, signed with the new key, applies and preserves it. |
| `TestDistributionRejectsLocalNodeRemoval` | A bundle removing the local node is rejected; the timestamp stays unchanged. |
| `TestDistributionRejectsInvalidCentralConfig` | An invalid bundle is rejected. |
| `TestHealthcheckPing` | Two nodes anycast a ping-checked /32 and fail over by metric. |
| `TestHealthcheckHTTP` | An HTTP-checked service IP fails over from backup (static metric 10,000,000 µs = 10 s) to primary (HTTP metric 10) when the server starts. |
| `TestJSONLogging` | `--json` emits slog JSON records. |
| `TestIPCRawSocketJSONHasNoErrnoTrailer` | A raw UAPI `get=nylon` returns pure protojson with no errno trailer. |
| `TestTunDropReproduction1CPU` | A 1-CPU node pushes eight iperf3 streams through `nylon0`; its `tx_dropped` grows by at most 50 over 15 s while the run carries ≥ 1e8 bit/s. |
| `TestTunDropFree4CPU` | Four CPUs and twelve streams: the same bound on `tx_dropped` growth and throughput floor. |

### Continuous Integration

CI is `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, triggered on every push and PR to `main` (ignoring changes under `docs/**` and `README.md`, cancelling in-progress runs per ref) with seven jobs: `lint` (golangci-lint), `unit_test`, `integration`, and `e2e` — CI runs the same test commands as the local targets, directly through the pinned runner `go run gotest.tools/gotestsum@v1.13.0` rather than `make`, with e2e parallelism set to the runner's `$(nproc)` — plus `licenses` (regenerates `NOTICE`/`licenses/` and fails on any `git diff`), `release_config` (`goreleaser check`), and a push-only `cross_build` compile matrix that also compiles `windows/amd64` as a canary. Every job pins Go through `go-version-file: go.mod`.

## Container Images

The `nylon-lb` load balancer ships as a container image, built from `cmd/nylon-lb/Dockerfile.dev` — a `golang:1.26.3` builder, a `scratch` `runtime` stage with `EXPOSE 9633`, and an `ubuntu:24.04` `debug` stage with `curl`, `iproute2`, and `tcpdump`. (The plain `cmd/nylon-lb/Dockerfile` is GoReleaser-only: its build context is prebuilt release binaries, not the source tree.)

```bash
# runtime variant
make image-nylon-lb

# debug variant (extra tooling)
make image-nylon-lb-debug

# push to your registry
REGISTRY=ghcr.io/yourorg make push-nylon-lb
```

The targets take these variables:

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `REGISTRY` | — | Registry to push to (`push-nylon-lb`). |
| `IMAGE_NAME` | `nylon-lb` | Image repository name. |
| `IMAGE_TAG` | `$(VERSION)` | Image tag; defaults to the stamped version. |
| `PLATFORMS` | `linux/amd64,linux/arm64` | Multi-arch build platforms. |
| `IMAGE_EXTRA_ARGS` | — | Extra flags passed through to the image build. |

For what the balancer actually does at runtime, see the [nylon-lb guide](/guides/nylon-lb).

The root `Dockerfile` (for the nylon daemon itself) has two relevant stages: the `runtime` stage is `FROM scratch` with `ENTRYPOINT nylon run` and `WORKDIR /app/config`, while the `debug` stage adds `-v -w --dbg-trace-tc` to the entrypoint for verbose, traced runs — handy when you are [troubleshooting](/guides/troubleshooting) a live mesh.

## Release Process

The `release.yml` workflow triggers on a `v*` tag and runs GoReleaser, which publishes:

- Raw binaries of **`nylon`** and **`nylon-genesis`** (loose executables named `nylon-linux-amd64` and so on, not archives) for Linux (`386`, `amd64`, `arm64`) and macOS (`amd64`, `arm64`; no `386`).
- A license meta-archive `nylon-licenses_<version>.tar.gz` (`LICENSE`, `LICENSE.GPL-3.0`, `NOTICE`, `polyamide/LICENSE`, `licenses/`) and `checksums.txt`.
- The **`nylon-lb`** container image `ghcr.io/arsolitt/nylon/nylon-lb` (Linux `amd64`/`arm64`), tagged with the release version; stable, non-prerelease releases also get the `latest` image tag, while `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` tags publish GitHub pre-releases.

There are no Windows release artifacts — `windows/amd64` is compiled in CI as a canary only. `nylon-genesis` ships as raw release binaries, and `nylon-lb` ships as a container image only; build its raw binary from source with `make nylon-lb` if you need it.

Version stamping works through `internal/buildinfo`: the defaults are `Version='dev'` and `Commit='none'`, and `make build` overrides both via `-ldflags -X` using `git describe` and `git rev-parse`. If a binary was built inside a git tree without explicit stamps, `nylon version` falls back to `debug.ReadBuildInfo` and reports the `vcs.revision`, truncated to 8 characters.

## Demo Tooling

The `demo/` directory packages a self-contained mesh stand (alice, bob, charlie) plus the recorder that produces the demo assets used by this site. Both entry points need only Docker with Compose v2 and `python3` — everything else runs inside the image:

```bash
./demo/up.sh      # stand up and leave it running
./demo/record.sh  # record the failover assets into docs/assets/
```

- **`demo/lib.sh`** — shared helpers: paths, the `docker compose` wrapper, subnet picking (a free `10.2xx.y.0/24` from the same pool the e2e harness uses) and the next-hop query against the daemon's own route table.
- **`demo/generate-configs.sh`** — writes `demo/.env`, three keypairs and the central/node configs, then validates them with `nylon verify`. Idempotent; `--force` regenerates.
- **`demo/up.sh`** — the documented one command: configs, `docker compose up`, then a bounded wait until alice really reaches charlie through the mesh. Prints the next hop per node and leaves the stand running.
- **`demo/record.sh`** — records the failover end to end: a 140x35 `tmux` layout running `mtr`, `ping`, alice's forwarding table and the story pane, recorded with asciinema, converted with `agg` and installed into `docs/assets/demo.{cast,gif}`. `--no-install` keeps the files in `demo/output/`.
- **`demo/panes/`** — the four pane scripts, copied into the container by the recorder. The story pane cuts the `alice`–`charlie` link with `iptables`, then asserts each transition by polling alice's route table — a `PASS` line per step, and a run that never observed the reroute fails instead of printing a success.

Three properties of the stand are worth knowing before changing it. Alice's link to bob is shaped to 20ms (`pre_up` in the generated `alice.yaml`), because on a docker bridge every link measures the same sub-millisecond latency with comparable jitter — without the shaping the mesh re-selects routes on noise and the failover timing is a coin flip. The stand is then warmed up with one cut/restore cycle before anything is recorded (`warm_up` in `lib.sh`, also run by `up.sh`), because the algorithm only accepts the backup route while the mesh reconverges: a cold mesh can otherwise sit without it and turn a ~6s reroute into a ~45s one. And the story pane asserts that state itself — it waits for the direct route and for bob advertising `10.99.0.3/32` before cutting anything.

The recorder is the gate: a green run proves the reroute happened and leaves the assets the README and the [docs landing page](/) render. Tear the stand down with `docker compose --env-file demo/.env -f demo/docker-compose.yml -p nylon-demo down --remove-orphans`.
---
url: /reference/config
---
# Configuration Reference

## node.yaml

Each node has its own `node.yaml` with local settings. Generate a keypair with `nylon key`. Stdout is the private key, stderr is the public key.

```yaml
key: 0NcrMcaS1tORCTA88L5ZPE+H6yUMV4e5vRp6iypnPW8= # private key (from `nylon key`)
id: alice # must match this node's id in central.yaml
port: 57175 # UDP port nylon listens on

# --- Optional fields below ---

use_system_routing: false # if true, all peer packets exit via the TUN interface
no_tun: false # if true, run as a userspace-only relay without a TUN (requires use_system_routing: false and no addresses/prefixes for this node in central.yaml)
no_net_configure: false # if true, nylon won't touch system routes or interfaces
log_path: "" # write logs to this file (empty = stderr only)
interface_name: "" # override the interface name (default: "nylon", or utunX on macOS)
dns_resolvers: [] # DNS servers for nylon's own lookups, e.g. ["1.1.1.1:53"]
observability_addr: "" # e.g. "0.0.0.0:9090"; enables /metrics, /healthz, /readyz, and /discovery
mtu: 1420 # TUN interface MTU (omit for the device default 1420)
tun_queues: 4 # TUN queues drained in parallel (default: min(CPU count, 4)); Linux only
tun_txqueuelen: 10000 # kernel tx queue length per TUN queue (default: 10000; 0 = kernel default 500)
tun_backpressure: false # request IFF_BACKPRESSURE (default: false; requires kernel >= 6.15)
dynamic_prefixes_dir: "" # directory watched for dynamic prefix JSON files, e.g. /etc/nylon/prefixes.d (empty = disabled)

# Bootstrap: fetch central.yaml from a remote bundle on first start
dist:
  url: https://static.example.com/network1.nybundle
  key: 7PaN6DmAayz4KnDnsXSXJH+Oy0TFGeoM4FEbQfLriVY= # distribution public key

# Split tunneling (per-node overrides)
exclude_ips: # add to the central exclude list
  - 192.168.0.0/24
unexclude_ips: [] # subtract from the central exclude list

# Lifecycle hooks (run in order)
pre_up: []
pre_down: []
post_up:
  - iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 192.168.0.0/24 -j MASQUERADE
post_down: []
```

The `tun_*` fields size the TUN datapath and apply on Linux only; every other platform keeps the single-queue path. `tun_queues` drains the interface from several queues in parallel — the kernel steers each flow to one queue, so per-flow packet order is preserved and more queues mean more CPU parallelism for the drain. `tun_txqueuelen` is the kernel burst buffer the daemon reads from (one packet per unit, roughly 1.4 KB of kernel memory per queue at MTU 1420); it is programmed at interface creation and only takes effect when more than one queue is created. `tun_backpressure` asks the kernel to stop dropping when a queue is full and let the qdisc queue instead, trading dropped packets for added latency; it needs kernel >= 6.15 and is otherwise a silent no-op. Both counts are validated when the config is loaded: `tun_queues` must be 1–32 and `tun_txqueuelen` 0–1048576.

When you set `dynamic_prefixes_dir`, the nylon daemon watches that directory and announces prefixes from JSON files that local writers (scripts, Kubernetes sidecars, the nylon-lb agent) place there. See [Dynamic Prefixes](/reference/dynamic-prefixes) for the file contract.

---

## central.yaml

The central config defines the entire network topology. It is shared across all nodes (either copied manually or via config distribution).

```yaml
# --- Config Distribution (optional) ---
dist:
  # The distribution key is used to verify and decrypt sealed bundles.
  # Despite being called "public", treat it as a shared secret. It can decrypt your topology.
  key: 7PaN6DmAayz4KnDnsXSXJH+Oy0TFGeoM4FEbQfLriVY=
  # Nylon polls these URLs every 10 seconds for config updates
  repos:
    - file:central.nybundle          # local file
    - https://static.example.com/network1.nybundle # remote URL (HTTP GET)

# --- Routers ---
# Active nylon nodes that participate in routing and can forward traffic.
routers:
  - id: alice
    pubkey: xmfAovAKN4AY5ocK5s+/VsG9I27KrQ13Vzb0HOsLKAs=
    addresses: [10.0.0.1] # nylon interface addresses (auto-advertised as /32 or /128)
    endpoints:
      - "alice.example.com:57175" # domain name (re-resolved periodically)
      - "192.168.1.2:57175"       # LAN IP
    prefixes:
      # Static: always advertised at the given metric
      - type: static
        prefix: 192.168.0.0/24
        metric: 0 # optional, default 0

      # Ping: advertised with RTT as metric, withdrawn after max_failures consecutive failures
      - type: ping
        prefix: 10.1.0.0/24
        addr: 10.1.0.8           # address to ping
        delay: 10s               # interval between pings (default: 15s)
        max_failures: 3          # failures before withdrawal (default: 3)
        bind_if: en10            # optional: bind to a specific interface
        # metric: 0              # optional: override RTT with a static metric (advertised unconditionally; suppresses failure retraction)

      # HTTP: advertised with request duration as metric, withdrawn on non-200 response
      - type: http
        prefix: 10.2.0.0/24
        url: http://example.com/healthz
        delay: 15s               # interval between probes (default: 15s)
        # metric: 5              # optional: override request duration with a static metric

  - id: bob
    pubkey: 4GfHHSyVpXc+wkbjyIIONERa6Xf5EafB0nVGZLf2r2o=
    addresses: [10.0.0.2, 10.1.0.2] # multiple addresses are fine
    endpoints:
      - "192.168.1.1:57175"
      - "nylon.example.org" # port defaults to 57175 (the nylon default port)
    # Optional per-node obfuscation params. They apply only to this node's
    # sender path (receivers ignore them) and are normally generated by
    # `nylon genesis`.
    # obf:
    #   protocol: quic # informational template name (quic|dns|dtls|stun|sip|rtp|random)
    #   i1: <b 0xc0ff><r 8><t><r 40> # CPS spec; i2-i5 are optional, empty ones are omitted

  - id: eve
    pubkey: 2mXTTD+FYdtJm/v1vSHz8qimvCucjW9vY+nLYacXJFE=
    addresses: [10.0.0.3]
    # no endpoints. eve can only connect outward to nodes that have endpoints

  - id: public
    pubkey: dJcUE1qnXCQ5x8pMhFb/MZab7YrBaaHcrgfbmQI0MW4=
    addresses: [10.0.0.4]
    endpoints:
      - "123.123.123.123:57175" # multiple endpoints; nylon picks the best one dynamically
      - "123.123.123.124:57175"

# --- Clients ---
# Passive WireGuard clients that don't run nylon. Only static prefixes allowed.
clients:
  - id: client1
    pubkey: SBI+yvF30Ba4xo0GKTtKHSSfbXAnRNFTBwydJyJp6Rk=
    addresses: [10.0.0.7]
    prefixes:
      - type: static
        prefix: 192.168.1.0/24 # also add this to AllowedIPs in the WireGuard client config

# --- Split Tunnel ---
# Excluded prefixes are NOT routed through nylon (network-wide default).
# Per-node overrides are in node.yaml (exclude_ips / unexclude_ips).
#
# How the layers combine (applied per-node):
# 1. Start with all prefixes from the routing table
# 2. Drop: prefixes this node itself originates (exact match only --
#    learned more-specifics inside them still install)
# 3. Subtract: central exclude_ips (below)
# 4. Add back: node unexclude_ips
# 5. Subtract: node exclude_ips
#
# Example: central excludes 10.0.0.0/8. Node "alice" sets
# unexclude_ips: [10.1.0.0/16] -- re-includes 10.1.x.x
# exclude_ips: [10.1.99.0/24] -- but not 10.1.99.x
# Result for alice: 10.1.0.0/16 is routed through nylon, except 10.1.99.0/24.
# All other 10.x.x.x traffic bypasses nylon.
exclude_ips:
  - 192.168.0.0/24

# --- Dynamic Prefix Ranges ---
# Receiver-side allowance for prefixes.d announcements: receivers accept an
# announced prefix when it falls inside one of these ranges (prefixes already
# listed under routers[] remain routable regardless). Each range must be a
# valid, masked prefix (no host bits). Empty = fail-closed: only prefixes
# known from this central config are routable.
dynamic_prefix_ranges:
  - 10.0.0.0/8

# --- Obfuscation ---
# Mesh-wide AmneziaWG 2.0 profile. Central placement keeps the S and H
# parameters identical on every node by construction, which the wire format
# requires. Omit the whole block for vanilla WireGuard-compatible behavior.
# The values below are examples; generate a profile with `nylon genesis`.
obf:
  jc: 5
  jmin: 250 # must not exceed jmax
  jmax: 800
  s1: 32
  s2: 28
  s3: 20
  s4: 16
  h1: # header range: min must not exceed max
    min: 100
    max: 5000000
  h2: # header ranges must not overlap each other
    min: 10000000
    max: 200000000
  h3:
    min: 400000000
    max: 800000000
  h4:
    min: 1000000000
    max: 2100000000

# --- Graph ---
# Defines which nodes will peer with each other. Only nodes connected in the graph
# will attempt to establish WireGuard tunnels.
#
# IMPORTANT: The graph controls direct peering only. Two nodes that are NOT
# directly connected in the graph can still communicate. Their traffic is
# forwarded through intermediate nodes that ARE connected.
graph:
  # Groups: a shorthand for sets of nodes (nodes within a group are NOT auto-connected)
  - Group1 = alice, bob
  - Group1, Group1           # connect every node in Group1 to every other node in Group1
  - Group2 = Group1, client1 # groups can contain other groups
  - client1, eve, alice      # all three fully interconnected

# Updated automatically by `nylon seal`; used as a version number for config distribution.
timestamp: 1740832962209309000
```

A `metric` override behaves differently per check type. On a `ping` entry the value is advertised unconditionally from startup and suppresses failure retraction, so the prefix stays announced even when the probe target is down; leave it unset if you want health-driven withdrawal. On an `http` entry the override replaces only the healthy request-duration metric, and failures still retract. See [Dynamic Prefixes](/reference/dynamic-prefixes) for the full behavior.

The `obf` profile and the per-node `i1`-`i5` specs are normally produced by `nylon genesis`, which picks viable header ranges automatically. See [Obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation) for the wire-format background and [Genesis](/guides/genesis) for the generation workflow.

---

## Obfuscation Fields

Two independent `obf` blocks exist. The mesh-wide profile sits at the top level of `central.yaml`; per-node params sit under each `routers[]` entry (and are also accepted under `clients[]`, although `nylon genesis` emits them for routers only).

### central.yaml `obf` (mesh-wide profile)

| Field   | Type                            | Default             | Constraints                                                                                                        |
| ------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `jc`    | uint32                          | `0`                 | —                                                                                                                  |
| `jmin`  | uint32                          | `0`                 | must not exceed `jmax`                                                                                             |
| `jmax`  | uint32                          | `0`                 | —                                                                                                                  |
| `s1`-`s4` | uint32                        | `0`                 | —                                                                                                                  |
| `h1`-`h4` | map with `min`/`max` (uint32) | `min: 0`, `max: 0`  | `min` must not exceed `max` within a range; ranges must not overlap (the device rejects overlaps at UAPI apply time with `headers must not overlap`) |

Each `h1`-`h4` range maps to the AmneziaWG UAPI `min-max` form. Omitting the entire `obf` block keeps vanilla WireGuard-compatible header values (`h1` through `h4` pinned to `1-1`, `2-2`, `3-3`, and `4-4`). Ranges that `nylon genesis` generates avoid WireGuard message type ids 1-4.

### routers[].obf (per-node, sender-local)

| Field      | Type   | Default             | Notes                                                                                                          |
| ---------- | ------ | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `protocol` | string | omitted             | Informational AmneziaWG template name: `quic`, `dns`, `dtls`, `stun`, `sip`, `rtp`, or `random`                 |
| `i1`-`i5`  | string | omitted when empty  | CPS packet specs such as `<b 0xc0ff><r 8><t><r 40>`; only non-empty specs are emitted                           |

Receivers ignore `protocol` and `i1`-`i5`: these params shape only how this node's outgoing packets look, while the mesh-wide profile governs the receiving side.

---

## Dynamic Prefixes (prefixes.d)

Setting `dynamic_prefixes_dir` in `node.yaml` (recommended: `/etc/nylon/prefixes.d`) enables a watcher that announces prefixes from JSON files in that directory:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "prefixes": [
    { "type": "static", "prefix": "10.99.0.1/32", "metric": 0 }
  ]
}
```

The contract:

- `version` must be `1`; `prefixes` entries use the same `type` values and keys as the central `prefixes` list (`static`, `ping`, `http`).
- Adding or updating a file announces its prefixes; removing it withdraws them.
- Invalid JSON or an unsupported version skips the whole file; a single invalid entry skips only that entry.
- Files apply in lexicographic filename order; a duplicate prefix across files resolves to the entry from the earlier filename.
- Use one writer per file, and write to a temp file followed by an atomic rename (the temp name must not end in `.json`).
- On the receiving side, announcements are gated by central `dynamic_prefix_ranges`.

See [Dynamic Prefixes](/reference/dynamic-prefixes) for the full contract and examples.

---

## Naming Rules

Node IDs (`routers[].id`, `clients[].id`) must:
- Match `^[0-9a-z._/-]+$`
- Be at most 100 characters
- Be unique across all routers and clients

Group names used in `graph` are folded to lowercase, must not equal a node name, and must be unique. The strict node-ID pattern above is not applied to them.
---
url: /reference/dynamic-prefixes
---
# Dynamic Prefixes

Dynamic prefixes let you add and remove advertised prefixes while a node is running. Instead of editing the central config and reloading, you drop JSON files into a directory the daemon watches, and nylon announces the prefixes into the mesh using the normal Babel routing machinery. Deleting a file retracts the announcement.

The feature has two halves:

- The **announcing node** watches its `dynamic_prefixes_dir` for `*.json` files and announces every valid prefix they describe, alongside the static prefixes from its central config.
- Every **receiving node** accepts an announced dynamic prefix only if it falls inside its own central `dynamic_prefix_ranges` (or exactly matches a prefix it already knows). The default is fail-closed: with no ranges declared, receivers drop every dynamic announcement.

## Configuration

Two YAML keys control the feature. Both are optional; the feature is fully disabled unless you set the directory.

| Key | Config level | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dynamic_prefixes_dir` | node | string | `""` (disabled) | Directory the daemon watches for `*.json` prefix files. The recommended location is `/etc/nylon/prefixes.d`. |
| `dynamic_prefix_ranges` | central | list of CIDR prefixes | `[]` (fail-closed) | Receiver-side allowance: prefixes a node accepts from peers' dynamic announcements. Ranges must be valid and masked. |

**node config**

```yaml
# Enables the watcher on this node only.
dynamic_prefixes_dir: /etc/nylon/prefixes.d
```

**central config**

```yaml
# Allow dynamic announcements for pod CIDRs and the anycast VIP slice.
dynamic_prefix_ranges:
  - 10.42.0.0/16
  - 10.60.0.0/24
```

Cross-node routing needs both halves: the announcer needs `dynamic_prefixes_dir` to announce, and every receiver needs a `dynamic_prefix_ranges` entry that covers the announced prefix. A receiver accepts an announced prefix when the prefix is **equal to one of its central prefixes** or **a subnet of one of the declared ranges**. Supernets of a declared range are rejected. The gate applies to route updates, ack-retracts, and seqno-requests alike.

See the [config reference](/reference/config) for how these keys fit into the full node and central configs.

## File contract

The watched directory contains flat `*.json` files (subdirectories are ignored). Each file holds a schema-versioned list of prefix entries:

**prefixes.d/10-vip.json**

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "prefixes": [
    {"type": "static", "prefix": "10.42.1.0/24", "metric": 0},
    {"type": "ping", "prefix": "10.1.0.0/24", "addr": "10.1.0.8",
     "delay": "10s", "max_failures": 3, "bind_if": "", "metric": 5},
    {"type": "http", "prefix": "10.2.0.0/24", "url": "http://example.com/healthz",
     "delay": "15s", "metric": 5}
  ]
}
```

The schema is a field-for-field mirror of the prefix health config (`StaticPrefixHealth`, `PingPrefixHealth`, `HTTPPrefixHealth`), so dynamic prefixes support the same health checks as static prefixes.

| Field | Type | Applies to | Required | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `version` | int | file | yes | — | Must be `1`. Any other value skips the whole file. |
| `prefixes` | array | file | yes | — | List of prefix entries. |
| `type` | string | entry | yes | — | Discriminator: `static`, `ping`, or `http`. |
| `prefix` | string (CIDR) | entry | yes | — | The prefix to announce. Must be masked — host bits set are a per-entry error. |
| `metric` | uint32 | all | no | `0` (static); health-derived (ping/http) | For `static`: the advertised metric. For `ping`/`http`: overrides the health-derived metric. |
| `addr` | string (IP) | `ping` | yes for `ping` | — | Address to ping. |
| `max_failures` | int | `ping` | no | `3` | Failed probe round withdraws the prefix. |
| `delay` | Go duration string | `ping`, `http` | no | `15s` | Interval between probes. Also used as the HTTP request timeout for `http` checks. |
| `bind_if` | string | `ping` | no | `""` (all interfaces) | Local interface to bind the ping to. |
| `url` | string | `http` | yes for `http` | — | URL to GET. |

Durations use Go syntax: `10s`, `1m30s`, `500ms`.

:::caution
The JSON path skips the validation applied to prefixes declared in the central config, which rejects a `delay` of zero or less and a `max_failures` of zero or less. In `prefixes.d` these values pass through unchecked: a `delay` of `0s` or a negative duration panics the monitor goroutine inside `time.NewTicker`, and a `max_failures` of `0` panics the ping loop with an integer divide-by-zero — either panic crashes the daemon. A negative `max_failures` does not panic, but every probe round fails (`zero attempts`) and the prefix can never become healthy. Writers must validate both values before writing a file.
:::

### Parsing rules

Parsing is fail-closed at two levels:

- **Whole file skipped**: malformed JSON, a top-level non-object, or an unsupported `version`. A file read error skips that file too. Other files still apply.
- **Single entry skipped**: unparseable or unmasked `prefix`, an unknown `type`, a `ping` entry without a valid `addr`, an `http` entry without a `url`, or an invalid `delay`. Remaining entries in the same file still apply.

Every skip is logged with the file name and entry index.

## Runtime behavior

- **Startup**: the daemon scans the directory, snapshots the pristine central config, and injects the parsed prefixes into its own node entry — all before the first routing reconcile, so the merged view is what the mesh sees first. A scan failure never blocks startup. Injection only happens if the node has an entry in the central config; a node absent from `routers`/`clients` announces nothing.
- **Watching**: an fsnotify watcher fires on any change in the directory. After a 250 ms debounce (the timer resets on every event), the daemon fully rescans the directory and re-applies the pristine central config with the fresh dynamic set injected. If the directory is removed or the watcher cannot be created, the watcher stops and logs an error; the feature stays disabled until restart.
- **Withdrawal**: deleting a file, emptying it, or breaking its JSON removes its prefixes from the merged set, and the existing Babel retraction machinery withdraws the announcements.
- **Central config interplay**: injection happens inside `ApplyCentralConfig` after central-only validation and before the no-op check. The central config polls for updates every 10 s; each apply re-injects the dynamic set from the pristine snapshot, so central updates never clobber dynamic state. A steady state with unchanged files is a no-op.

## Conflict rules

| Situation | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Entry's prefix already exists in the central config for this node | Entry rejected with an error log — the central config wins. |
| Same prefix in two `*.json` files, or twice in one file | The first entry in scan order wins (lexicographic filename order, top-to-bottom within a file); the later entry is rejected with a warning whose text says the duplicate is "across files", even within a single file. |
| Malformed JSON or unsupported `version` | Whole file skipped with an error; other files still apply. |
| Invalid single entry | Only that entry is skipped; the rest of the file applies. |

Number your files by writer to make the ordering deterministic (see [Writers](#writers)).

## Health checks

Dynamic `ping` and `http` prefixes reuse the full prefix-health monitor machinery, not just static advertisement.

| Check | Probe | Healthy metric | Failed probe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `static` | none | configured `metric` (default `0`) | never fails — always advertised |
| `ping` | ICMP ping of `addr` every `delay`; up to `max_failures` attempts, each timing out after `delay`/`max_failures`, stopping early on success | ping RTT in microseconds (or `metric` override) | prefix retracted (infinite metric) |
| `http` | HTTP GET of `url` every `delay`; request timeout equals `delay` | request duration in microseconds (or `metric` override) | prefix retracted (infinite metric) |

Details worth knowing:

- Both monitors start retracted (infinite metric) and join the mesh after the first successful probe — unless a `ping` entry sets `metric`: its override is advertised immediately from startup and never retracts. An `http` entry with `metric` still starts retracted; the override replaces only the healthy-path metric.
- An `http` check fails on a transport error or any non-200 status code.
- A failed probe round logs a warning and retracts the prefix through the normal Babel retraction path; a later successful round re-announces it.

:::caution
The `metric` override behaves differently per check type. On a `ping` entry, nylon advertises the fixed value unconditionally and ignores the live RTT-derived metric — including failure retraction, so the prefix stays announced even when the probe target is down. On an `http` entry, the override replaces only the healthy request-duration metric; a failed probe still retracts the prefix even with `metric` set. Leave `metric` unset on `ping` entries if you want health-driven withdrawal; an `http` entry retracts on failure either way.
:::

## Security model

`prefixes.d` is an **unauthenticated local control surface**: anyone who can write a `*.json` file into the directory controls what the node announces. Nylon does not check file permissions itself, so harden the directory at the OS level:

- Root-owned directory with `0755`, root-owned files with `0644`.
- Only trusted writers (root, or a hostPath-mounted agent) can write to the directory.

Writers must replace files atomically: write to a temp file, then rename it over the final name. The temp file name **must not end in `.json`** — the daemon globs `*.json`, so a partially written temp file with that suffix would be parsed mid-write. Rename-into-directory is also what reliably triggers the fsnotify watcher.

## Writers

Files follow a one-writer-per-file convention. Give each writer its own file name so ownership and lexicographic tie-breaking stay deterministic, for example `10-podcidr.json` for a k8s sidecar.

### nylon-lb

The `nylon-lb` LoadBalancer agent is the reference writer. For each `type=LoadBalancer` Service it writes `lb-<namespace>-<name>.json` with a static `/32` entry:

**prefixes.d/lb-default-my-service.json**

```json
{"version":1,"prefixes":[{"type":"static","prefix":"10.60.0.100/32","metric":0}]}
```

It writes atomically (temp file, `0644`, rename), skips rewrites when the content is unchanged, and garbage-collects only files matching `lb-*.json` — it never touches files owned by other writers, such as `00-vip.json` or `10-podcidr.json`. Note that its pool must sit inside every receiver's `dynamic_prefix_ranges`, or the announcements are dropped. See the [nylon-lb guide](/guides/nylon-lb) for deployment.

### Manual VIP announcement

For a single anycast VIP without Kubernetes, use the reference systemd pattern: a `nylon-vip.service` unit that owns one file, for example `prefixes.d/00-vip.json`, and binds the address to a local interface. Because the unit is the only writer of that file, updates and withdrawals stay race-free.

## Troubleshooting

If a node announces a dynamic prefix that peers never route, the receiver side is the usual suspect: without a matching `dynamic_prefix_ranges` entry the announcement is silently dropped, and the receiver logs a dropped-unknown-prefix warning throttled to once per hour per prefix. Check the announcer's logs for file-parse errors, and see the [troubleshooting guide](/guides/troubleshooting) for log locations and inspection commands.
---
url: /reference/passive-nodes
---
# Passive Nodes

Passive nodes (referred to as just `Clients` in the code) are standard WireGuard implementations that do not run the nylon daemon. They connect to the network via **Gateway Nodes**. In nylon, any node can serve as a gateway automatically, requiring no special configuration.

## Architecture

Unlike active routers that participate in the distance-vector protocol, passive nodes act as "stub" nodes. They are represented in the network by one or more gateway nodes that advertise their presence.

```mermaid
graph LR
    PN((Passive Node)) -- "Active Tunnel" --> GA[Gateway A]
    PN -. "Roaming Path" .-> GB[Gateway B]

    GA <--> Mesh([Other nylon nodes])
    GB <--> Mesh
```

### Connecting to a Gateway
When a passive node connects to a gateway, the gateway identifies it using its WireGuard public key (defined in `central.yaml`). A gateway creates the client's WireGuard peer only when the two are graph-adjacent (a `graph` edge in `central.yaml`), and it begins advertising all of the addresses and prefixes associated with that passive node on the central config only after receiving at least one authenticated packet from the client.

:::note

There are no health checks for the prefixes advertised by the passive node.

:::

### Seamless Roaming
Nylon supports seamless roaming for passive nodes. If a passive node switches its connection from Gateway `A` to Gateway `B`:
1. Gateway `B` detects the new connection and immediately begins advertising the node's IPs.
2. Gateway `A` detects that the passive node has stopped sending traffic and, about 6 s (`ClientDeadThreshold`) after the client's last packet, places the route into a "Passive Hold" state (see below), but only while it is the sole visible advertiser of the prefix and its own advertisement has not yet expired. If gateway `B`'s advertisement is already visible, `A` skips the hold and its advertisement lapses instead — `A` stops refreshing once the client is silent past `ClientDeadThreshold` and the competing advertisement is visible, and its advertisement is withdrawn roughly 8-10 seconds after the client's last packet to `A` (the last refresh sets a 3 s advertisement TTL, and the 1 s garbage collection removes it).
3. Gateway `A` observes the new advertisement from Gateway `B`, and preempts its own "held" route.
4. Gateway `A` stops advertising the node, allowing the network to converge on the path through Gateway `B`.

This allows mobile devices to switch between multiple VPN profiles (connected to different gateways) without losing connectivity to the internal network.

---

## Passive Hold

**Passive Hold** is an optimization designed to keep mobile devices and battery-constrained clients reachable even when they go silent.

:::note[Problem: Silent Clients]

Prior to Passive Hold, if a passive node stops sending packets (e.g., a mobile phone goes to sleep), the gateway does not know whether the client is still present or has disconnected. After a certain timeout, the gateway expires the route to that client and stops advertising it to the rest of the network.

This means:
1. If the client wakes up and tries to reconnect, it has to wait for route propagation again.
2. In order to keep connections alive, the client would need to send frequent keepalives, which can drain battery.

:::

To solve this, when a passive node goes silent, the gateway enters a "Passive Hold" state for that node. The gateway continues to advertise the client's prefixes, but at a metric of `INFM / 2` (where `INFM` = `0xFFFFFFFE`, so the hold metric is `2,147,483,647`). This allows the route to remain active in the network, but ensures that any new connection from the client to another gateway will take precedence.

Passive hold is driven by built-in defaults rather than configuration fields: `ClientKeepaliveInterval` is the advertisement TTL (3 s), `ClientDeadThreshold` is the silence after which a client counts as gone (6 s, twice `ClientKeepaliveInterval`), `ProbeDelay` is the passive scan cadence (1 s), and `GcDelay` is the garbage collection cadence (1 s).

At the same time, if the gateway detects any new advertisement for that client from another gateway, it stops refreshing its own "held" route. The advertisement expires `ClientKeepaliveInterval` (3 s) after its last refresh and is removed by the garbage collector (1 s cadence), so the prefix is withdrawn within roughly 4 s rather than instantly. This allows for seamless roaming without the need for keepalives.

---

## Miscellaneous Notes

Nylon does support advanced routing features for passive nodes, such as **anycast**. However, there are some important caveats to be aware of when using passive nodes.
1. Anycast passive nodes will stop having their prefixes advertised when they go silent. This can lead to suboptimal routing or oscillations if the passive node sends data over a long interval. You should consider enabling keepalives for anycast nodes to ensure they remain active in the network. (Keepalives must arrive within `ClientDeadThreshold` (6 s, with scans every 1 s) to keep the advertisement refreshed. Use e.g. 5 s; staying below `ClientKeepaliveInterval` (3 s) is the conservative bound.)
2. Passive nodes cannot advertise the same prefix as the gateway itself, or any other client which might be connected to the same gateway. This is because there is no easy way to determine which client is best.
3. Due to passive hold, there will always be a gateway advertising the client's prefixes, even if the client is turned off. (Assuming the gateway is still active and the client has been heard since the gateway started: the hold bootstraps from a live advertisement, so a client that has not sent a packet since a gateway restart is simply not advertised.) This means that if a client is truly offline, the route will be effectively blackholed.

The **Passive Hold** state is visible in the CLI and discovery surfaces: `nylon status` marks client neighbours with `[passive client]` and held advertisements with `passive-hold`, and the discovery endpoint reports `nylon_node_type=passive` for client nodes. Because `INFM / 2` is well below `INFM`, a held metric still renders numerically (`2147483647`) rather than as `INF`.
---
url: /gotchas
---
# Gotchas

A curated list of traps that bite operators and config authors — surprising defaults, silent ignores, fail-closed paths, and values that break the daemon. Each entry names the behavior (with the exact field, flag, or error you will see) and what to do about it; the linked guide or reference page has the full detail.

## Configuration

- **`port` is mandatory in `node.yaml` — `57175` is a convention, not a default.** `port: 0` fails validation with `port must be greater than 0`. The resolver default (`57175`) applies only when an endpoint string carries no port: a bare hostname or IP in `routers[].endpoints` silently gets `57175`, so a mismatched forwarded port fails with no diagnostic. Scheme URLs are rejected explicitly, and a non-numeric port fails with `invalid port`. See [Configuration Reference](/reference/config).

- **Sample keys are illustrative, not deployable.** The keys in the overview snippet and `example/` are public sample keypairs — the snippet's five keys decode and verify, which makes them copy-pasteable, but every node needs its own `nylon key` keypair, and the mesh-wide `obf` profile must match across all nodes. The shipped `example/sample-central.yaml` does not even pass validation: `nylon verify example/sample-central.yaml` exits 1 with `failed to decode public key (...): illegal base64 data at input byte 44`, and the `port` comment in `example/sample-node.yaml` (claiming `Default: 57175`) is convention, not a code default.

- **YAML parsing is silent about most mistakes — and keys are worse.** Unknown fields are ignored (there is no strict decoding), so a typo'd field name silently drops the setting, including AWG 3.x-only keys inside `obf`. Floats truncate into integer fields (`tun_queues: 2.5` becomes `2`), while duration fields reject bare numbers (`cannot unmarshal uint64 ... time.Duration`). An explicit `key: ""` panics during YAML decode instead of failing validation, and any base64 key that decodes to fewer than 32 bytes panics the same way; longer values are silently truncated to 32 bytes. Omitting the key entirely is the one form caught cleanly (`private key must not be empty`). Two knobs that never apply: `mtu` is not range-validated (an explicit `0` reaches TUN creation unchanged; omitting it means `1420`), and `tun_txqueuelen` only takes effect with more than one TUN queue.

- **`graph` and `verify` pitfalls.** A group-definition line (`Group = a, b, c`) creates no edges — write `Group, Group` to interconnect members or `X, Group` to pair X with each member. A missing or empty `graph` validates fine and produces no peering pairs. And `nylon verify` does not require every node to appear in the graph or check address uniqueness: a node omitted from `graph` verifies clean and ends up with zero peers, while a misspelled symbol is rejected (`invalid graph: <sym> is not a valid node/group`).

- **Hooks are not shell commands.** `pre_up`, `post_up`, `pre_down`, and `post_down` entries are split on single spaces and executed directly — no shell, no quoting, no pipes or globs. Failures are logged and do not abort startup or shutdown.

- **Reload does not mean "re-read my file".** Automatic config reload exists only when `central.yaml` has a `dist` block (repos are polled every 10 seconds); a manually edited local `central.yaml` is not re-read until `nylon reload` or a restart. `nylon reload --file` is accepted but completely ignored — the daemon always reloads its startup `-c` path — and a `REJECTED` apply exits 1 with an `Error:` line rather than printing `Result: REJECTED`. See [Troubleshooting](/guides/troubleshooting).

- **Endpoint resolution falls back silently.** If the `_nylon._udp` SRV lookup for an endpoint hostname fails — or the SRV target has no A/AAAA record — nylon silently uses the hostname's own addresses, with no log line at default levels (resolution failures only log `failed to resolve endpoint` at Debug). A wrong or stale SRV record therefore changes the effective endpoint invisibly; note that the 15-second re-resolution sweep only covers graph neighbours' endpoints.

## Obfuscation

- **An omitted `obf` block means vanilla-pinned header ranges.** With no `obf` in `central.yaml`, nylon synthesizes `h1=1-1`, `h2=2-2`, `h3=3-3`, `h4=4-4` to stay byte-compatible with vanilla WireGuard — it does not use the upstream AmneziaWG all-unset default (message type 0, itself incompatible with vanilla). The profile must be identical across the mesh: nodes carrying different `s`/`h` values fail to classify each other's packets and drop them silently, and hand-written S/H deviations — including an H range that overlaps `1..4` — pass config validation and silently change wire behavior. Profile changes apply live and cost one rekey window: every config apply re-runs the device IPC with the new profile, so in-flight handshakes can fail until all nodes converge on the new layout — treat a profile change as a maintenance action. See [Traffic Obfuscation](/guides/obfuscation).

- **Config validation is shallower than the device.** Range checks only enforce `min <= max` (and `jmin <= jmax`); overlapping header ranges are rejected by the device at apply time with `headers must not overlap`, surfaced as `failed to apply obf profile: ...` or `failed to configure wg device: ...` during daemon init or config sync. The deep invariants — padded-size collision classification and H-range viability — run only in `nylon-genesis`, so a hand-written profile with colliding sizes or an I length equal to a padded size can misclassify packets with no error anywhere.

- **AWG 3.x-only knobs fail loudly in one place and silently in another.** The device UAPI rejects `header_protection_key`, `content_padding_addition`, `random_trailers`, `disable_cookies`, `rekey_after_time`, `rekey_timeout`, `reject_after_time`, `keepalive_timeout`, and `max_handshake_attempts` with `AWG 3.x-only` — but writing the same keys inside `central.yaml`'s `obf` block parses with no error and does nothing.

- **I-pattern authoring is easy to get wrong silently.** An `i`-line with no `<...>` tags renders no packet and reports nothing; an unknown tag such as the kernel-only `<c>` fails at device configure time with `unknown tag <c>`, failing startup or reload; text outside tags is ignored. `<d>` and `<ds>` are rendered with no data source and contribute zero bytes (upstream AWG reuses values from earlier packets), so template shapes differ from upstream intent.

## Dynamic prefixes

- **Values that crash the daemon.** Central YAML health checks reject `delay <= 0` and `max_failures <= 0`, but the `prefixes.d` JSON path parses them unchecked and injection happens after validation. `delay: "0s"` (or a negative duration) panics inside `time.NewTicker`; `max_failures: 0` panics the ping goroutine with an integer divide-by-zero; both are unrecovered panics that abort the process. A negative `max_failures` does not panic, but every probe round fails (`zero attempts`) and the prefix can never become healthy. Validate before writing files. See [Dynamic Prefixes](/reference/dynamic-prefixes).

- **File-level rules decide what survives.** Malformed JSON, a top-level non-object, or an unsupported `version` skips the whole file — `version` is mandatory, and a missing one decodes as `0` and skips with `unsupported version 0`. A bad prefix, unknown `type`, missing `addr`/`url`, or invalid `delay` skips only that entry; unknown JSON fields are ignored without warning. Duplicate prefixes are resolved by filename: the lexicographically earlier file wins (the warning says "across files" even for duplicates inside one file), so a temp file named `*.json` that sorts first can win a conflict or be parsed mid-write — write to a non-`.json` temp name and rename.

- **A missing or unreadable `dynamic_prefixes_dir` disables the feature for the process lifetime.** Watcher creation failure only logs `cannot watch dynamic prefixes dir; feature disabled` — nothing retries, and the daemon never creates the directory. Fix the path and restart the daemon.

- **The receiver gate is silent and runs on every node.** Every node on the propagation path drops announcements outside its own `dynamic_prefix_ranges` — route updates, ack-retracts, and seqno-requests alike — leaving only a `received packet for unknown prefix` warning throttled to once per hour per prefix. Ranges must be masked (host bits are rejected with `invalid dynamic prefix range %s`), and an empty list is fail-closed: put the covering entry on every receiver, not just the final one.

- **Health-checked prefixes start retracted.** Both monitors store `INF` at construction and probe for the first time one `delay` after start (default `15s`), so a new file is not routable until a successful probe — except a `ping` entry with `metric`, whose override is advertised immediately and also disables failure retraction (the prefix stays announced while the target is down). An `http` entry with `metric` still retracts on a failed probe; its override replaces only the healthy-path metric. Ping infrastructure failures (bind-address or raw-socket errors) keep the last healthy RTT instead of retracting, and ping checks need root or `CAP_NET_RAW`.

## Config distribution

- **Repo URL forms are strict.** Only `file:`, `http`, and `https` are handled. A `file:` repo must use the opaque form `file:central.nybundle` — `file:/abs/path` and `file:///abs/path` fail with `failed to read file : ...` — and any other scheme leaves an empty body that later fails as `invalid bundle, too small`, wrapped in `failed to unbundle config from <repo>: ...`.

- **Fetches have no HTTP client timeout.** Each 10-second poll spawns one goroutine per repo, so a hung repo server leaks a goroutine per poll and stalls that repo's updates. Bundle bodies are truncated at `MaxConfigSize` (1 MiB), but only for http(s) — a local `file:` repo is read whole, with no size limit.

- **A mismatched signing key seals a bundle that only warns.** `nylon seal` proceeds when the private key does not match `dist.key`, logging `bundled public key differs from the signing key, check if this is intended!`. That warning is expected for the rotation transition bundle; otherwise it is a silent foot-gun — nodes that open the bundle with `dist.key` fail with `message authentication failed`.

- **Update outcomes are logged at different levels and mean different things.** A rejected or restart-required update logs `failed to apply central config update` as an error and keeps the old config; an update that committed but failed runtime reconciliation logs `central config applied with incomplete runtime reconciliation; will retry` as a warning and is already the active config. Fetch, unbundle, and validation failures log `Error updating config`. See [Config Distribution Setup](/guides/config-distribution).

## Passive clients

- **Graph adjacency is required, not just configuration.** WireGuard peers are created only for graph neighbours, so a client pointing at a node with no graph edge is never added as a peer and its handshakes are dropped. Even with an edge, the gateway advertises the client's prefix only after it has seen an authenticated packet from the client.

- **Keepalives must beat `ClientDeadThreshold` (6s).** With more than one advertiser the sole-advertiser hold is suppressed, and the advertisement lives only while traffic arrives within 6 seconds of a scan; a stock WireGuard persistent keepalive of `25s` is far too slow, and the last advertisement is gone roughly 8–10 seconds after the client's last packet. Use about `5s`, or stay below `ClientKeepaliveInterval` (3s) for the conservative bound. Any keepalive counts as client activity, and any other anycast advertiser of the prefix suppresses the hold too. See [Passive Nodes](/reference/passive-nodes).

- **Duplicate WireGuard pubkeys are silently mis-identified.** There is no pubkey-uniqueness validation, and lookup returns the first match with routers searched before clients — a router and a client (or two clients) sharing a key can bind passive detection to the wrong node.

- **Offline held clients are blackholed, not unreachable.** During a hold the gateway keeps a finite-metric route whose next hop is the client's WireGuard peer, so mesh traffic arrives at the gateway and is dropped when the client is offline — the prefix stays in the route table and looks routed. The held metric is forced to `INFM / 2` (`2147483647`) regardless of any static `metric` configured for the client.

## Kubernetes LoadBalancer

- **The shipped DaemonSet carries two traps.** It passes `--lb-class=nylon`: unclassed `type=LoadBalancer` Services stay `<pending>` for another controller, and only Services with `spec.loadBalancerClass=nylon` are claimed. It also does not wire `--node-name=$(NODE_NAME)`: without that flag the speaker falls back to the pod hostname, the single-announcer election never matches, and with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` nothing is announced. See [Kubernetes LoadBalancer](/guides/nylon-lb).

- **Pool specs fail at startup, and the errors are exact.** The spelling is `name=cidr` (`pool spec "bad" must be name=cidr (e.g. shared=10.110.0.0/24)`); `/31` and `/32` pools are rejected (`prefix length 31 leaves no usable host once the network and broadcast addresses are excluded`); only IPv4 pools are supported; an exclude outside every pool is fatal (`exclude "198.51.100.1" is outside every pool`). An `--exclude` applies to every pool whose CIDR contains the address, not to one chosen pool, and network/broadcast addresses pass the containment check but are never allocated.

- **The GC boundary is the filename.** Every `lb-*.json` in the prefixes directory that nylon-lb did not just desire is deleted on the next reconcile — files owned by other tooling (`00-vip.json`, `10-podcidr.json`) are safe, but any user file matching `lb-*.json` is not.

- **Fail-closed dynamics look like outages.** A Service-lister error makes the speaker treat every announce as stale: files are garbage-collected and all bound addresses enter the 60-second drain (recovery is automatic on a later pass). In single-announcer mode, announces are skipped while the local API view is more than 30 seconds stale (probed every 10 seconds), and a withdrawal removes the announce file immediately but keeps the `/32` bound for the 60-second drain.

- **`nylon_lb_announce_writes_total` counts reconcile calls, not file writes.** It advances even when the announce file's bytes are unchanged — in steady state about once per announced Service per reconcile (roughly every 30 seconds) with zero actual filesystem writes.

## Observability & metrics

- **`/healthz` is liveness only.** It returns 200 while the process runs even if the event loop is wedged; only shutdown turns it into a 503. The event-loop probe is `/readyz` and `/metrics` (1-second deadline, 503 on failure) — during a graceful shutdown those two return 503 with `not ready` / `metrics unavailable`, which is expected rather than a stall. See [Observability](/guides/observability).

- **Metric semantics that break naive queries.** `nylon_up` can never be `0` (it is rendered only after a successful snapshot), so scrape failures must be alerted with `up{job=...} == 0`. `nylon_endpoint_metric` reports `4294967295` (`INF`) for inactive endpoints, mixed with real microsecond values in the same label set, and its `endpoint` label is the configured endpoint string — possibly a hostname — not the resolved IP. A perf sample that fails to convert is silently skipped, so a `nylon_perf_*` series can vanish from `/metrics` with no log.

- **`/discovery` targets reuse the querying node's port.** Every target is built with the port from the querying node's own `observability_addr`, so nodes with different ports break discovery fleet-wide. Nodes with no address in `central.yaml` are silently omitted, and an empty mesh returns 200 with `[]`.

- **Debug and security.** `--dbg-perf` starts the performance web UI and `pprof` on `0.0.0.0:6060` — all interfaces. The observability server itself has no authentication or TLS, so bind it to a trusted interface or firewall it. A non-graceful Serve error on the observability listener cancels the daemon: an observability failure is a daemon failure.

## Routing & convergence

- **Selection is not plain lowest-metric.** A challenger must be more than ~9.1% better (`LinkSwitchDeadband = 1.1`), equal metrics keep the committed next hop, and a route committed less than `RouteSwitchHold` (5 seconds) ago is not displaced by a better candidate. Retracted routes (metric `INF`) bypass both damping rules, so recovery from a blackhole is immediate.

- **A retracted prefix is held as an exact-prefix blackhole.** The route stays in the table with metric `INF` and a blackhole forwarding entry until all connected neighbours ack-retract or the route expires (`RouteExpiryTime = 25s`). During that window `nylon status` shows the blackhole and traffic is dropped rather than falling back to a less-specific route — a covering aggregate does not rescue it.

- **Metric values are microseconds.** `HopCost` alone is 5, and a real 0.7 ms link is `700`. Until an endpoint has `MinimumConfidenceWindow = 15` samples (15 seconds at 1-second probes) it is scored pessimistically at 1 second (`1,000,000`); a measured ping of 0 maps to `100us`; `INF` is `4294967295`, with saturation at `INF - 1`.

- **Timing you must wait out.** A link is declared dead only after `LinkDeadThreshold = 5s` of silence, because probes are fire-and-forget (every 1 second, with no per-probe timeout). Inactive-endpoint recovery probes run every 1.5 seconds, discovery probes every 10 seconds, and state recomputes on probe replies and on GC every 1 second. When a source has no feasible route, starvation recovery broadcasts seqno requests every 100 ms at hop count 64 (deduped for 3 seconds), so routes can flap for seconds while the sequence-number cycle resolves.

- **Nylon is not Babel-on-the-wire.** It increases its own seqno by more than one on a seqno request (a documented RFC 8966 deviation, because it does not persist seqno state), and its control plane is a custom protobuf `Ny` message (protocol 8) — do not expect interoperability with other Babel implementations. Control messages coalesce into bundles up to `SafeMTU = 1200` and are sent high-priority; a single oversized message is still sent, fragmented.

- **Two silent behaviors.** OS route installation fails open: if the exclude IPSet cannot be built, nylon logs a warning and installs the unfiltered prefix set, widening the system routing table instead of dropping routes. And route updates are accepted only from graph neighbours, for known prefixes and router-ids; everything else is dropped, with unknown prefixes warned at most once per hour per prefix — a node missing from the central view silently filters its own control traffic.

## Building

- **Make targets.** There is no `make install` and no `make run`: the targets are `build`, `nylon`, `nylon-genesis`, `nylon-lb`, the `test*` suites, `image-*`/`push-nylon-lb`, `notice`, `proto`, and `clean`. `make build` emits `bin/nylon`, `bin/nylon-genesis`, and `bin/nylon-lb` with version/commit stamped from git, and `CGO_ENABLED=0` is exported by default. `make test` and `make test-integration` pass `--race`; `make test-e2e` does not (the containers run the plain binary), so race coverage claims do not extend to e2e. The e2e suite's `TestMain` builds the `nylon-debug:latest` image before every run, so first runs are slower and a build failure exits 1 with `Failed to build image`.

- **Build tags are load-bearing.** `sys_physical.go` is `//go:build !integration` and `sys_virtual.go` is `//go:build integration`, so `-tags=integration` swaps the sys layer. `go build ./...` compiles no tagged test helpers and not `interop/awgref`; the `awg_ref_interop` suite is manual-only: `go test -tags awg_ref_interop ./interop/awgref/ -v -count=1`.

- **Release and version alignment.** Release assets are loose executables named `<binary>-<os>-<arch>` (for example `nylon-linux-amd64`), not tarballs, and Windows is compiled in CI but never released. `nylon-lb --version` prints only `nylon-lb version <Version>` (`dev` for unstamped builds) — the commit appears in the startup log record. See [Building & Testing](/guides/development).
